kept.heading: MUSIC LICENSING CLAIMS ARE COMING FOR MARKETERS (6 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Music licensing claims are becoming a growing risk as brands and influencers use copyrighted content without proper clearance. Old social posts can also create exposure when licensing records are missing. Brands need to audit existing content and ensure influencer agreements cover licensing responsibilities.
kept.article_text:
Title: Music licensing claims are coming for marketers — is your organization ready? | Lockton

URL Source: https://global.lockton.com/us/en/news-insights/music-licensing-claims-are-coming-is-your-organization-ready

Markdown Content:
**Music licensing claims are coming for marketers — is your organization ready?**

Claims involving unlicensed music, videos, and other copyrighted content are becoming one of the fastest-growing intellectual property (IP) infringement exposures. Here's what organizations can do to reduce risk and strengthen their position with underwriters.

**A growing source of IP infringement risk**

Claims arising from the unauthorized use of music and other copyrighted content in digital marketing, social media, and advertising have become one of the most active and fastest-growing sources of IP infringement risk. Rights holders, which range from major labels to individual composers and publishers, are increasingly pursuing infringement claims tied to social media posts, influencer content and advertising campaigns that are using their unlicensed IP. Even historical content that organizations posted years ago and never revisited can be ripe for claims if prior agreements related to their use are not properly documented.

Several converging trends are driving an increasing risk for companies. These include:

*   **More frequent infringement claims.** A rights holder whose work is registered with the U.S. Copyright Office can claim statutory damages of $150,000 per infringement without showing loss. In most cases, insurers will deny a claim if “willful” infringement is alleged. Given the global nature of IP rights, claimants can often forum-shop.

*   Major rights holders continue to bring high-profile infringement actions, and once one major rights holder acts, others often follow.

*   **The decentralization of content creation.** Where advertising agencies once handled licensing reviews, content is now frequently created and posted directly by marketing teams and influencers, often without the same level of rights clearance. Where external agencies and individuals are engaged on behalf of a company, the management of this content can be challenging.

*   **Old content creating new problems.** Companies often keep videos and social posts produced over several years online in the public domain, often with little or no documentation showing whether music or other copyrighted content was properly licensed.

*   **Use of AI-generated content:** The ease of creating audio and visual content, which may be very clearly similar to that of third-party works, has increased the risk of infringement. AI-generated content is especially prevalent on social media, creating new risks for organizations and individuals. The increasing availability of cheap software to detect potentially infringing works has now made it much easier for rights holders to police infringing AI-generated content.

*   **Different approaches by individual insurers.** Some carriers exclude music-related claims altogether, while others continue to underwrite the exposure if insureds can demonstrate strong licensing and risk management practices. It is becoming increasingly common for insurers to exclude AI-generated content.

**What music licensing claims look like**

Music licensing claims can show up in several ways. Common sources of claims include the reposting of other people’s photos or videos without permission or credit; using full songs in content; and using copyright- and trademark-protected characters, logos, or artwork in merchandise, thumbnails or promotional material without licensing.

Some individuals and organizations may erroneously believe that giving credit — for example, tagging a creator with the comment “no copyright intended” — legal excuses use of that creator’s content, but it does not. Similarly, it should not be assumed that short clips constitute permissible fair use; this is is not an automatic defense to copyright infringement, as fair use is a fact-specific legal defense for purposes including criticism, commentary, news reporting, and teaching, but typically not marketing.

The following examples show where problems often start and what they can mean for insurance coverage.

*   A company's marketing team incorporates a popular sound recording into a promotional video without confirming that synchronization and master use rights had been secured. The rights holder later demands damages and threatens litigation. Insurance coverage may respond, but only if the policy includes IP infringement cover and does not contain a content exclusion.

*   A content audit uncovers older videos that a company had posted years earlier. The organization cannot locate licensing records, and therefore cannot verify whether rights have ever been secured. Carriers view these undocumented content libraries as a significant source of exposure and arguably as known risks that should be disclosed to underwriters prior to inception of a policy, likely resulting in exclusions.

*   A sports team, its venue, and event operators face a lawsuit on behalf of an artist tied to the broadcast of the artist’s music in a stadium during a sporting event without permission. Performance royalty organizations police venues and platforms on behalf of rights holders and often bring strategic litigation for improper use of their content.

*   A company launches an advertising campaign using music, videos, and images sourced from the internet without proper licenses. Media liability insurance coverage may respond to defense and settlement costs, subject to limits, but only where the claim is a content/IP dispute rather than a design or unfair competition issue.

*   A social media influencer posts a video promoting a retailer, which is the sued by a major music company, which alleging that its copyrighted music appeared in the promotional video without a license. Insurers increasingly point to influencer-created content as a growing source of claims activity.

**The questions underwriters are asking now**

During insurance program renewals, underwriters are increasingly asking organizations to demonstrate strong licensing controls when they seek access to broader coverage. One particular area of focus is the documentation of historical rights agreements, such as synchronizations rights that permit the use of a musical composition alongside visual media, or master use rights, which are agreements to the use of specific recordings.

Among other questions, your underwriter may ask:

*   When incorporating sound recordings into audio-visual works posted online, has your organization secured synchronization rights and master use licenses (including any “blanket” licenses)?

*   Has your organization searched and reviewed historical videos posted to its website or social media to confirm synchronization and master use rights, and removed any content for which rights cannot be confirmed?

*   Does your organization use music-scanning technology to continuously identify and remove infringing content from its website and social media presence?

*   Has your organization had a prior music licensing claim? If so, what remediation steps were taken?

*   Do your influencer agreements require the influencer to secure all rights to music and other third-party content?

*   Does your influencer agreement contain an indemnity clause to shift the copyright infringement to the influencer?

Being able to answer these questions affirmatively can help companies reduce litigation risk. It also improves their standing with underwriters at renewal, including enabling access to carriers without blanket music/licensing exclusions.

**Seven ways to reduce your exposure**

A few practical steps can help organizations avoid licensing problems and put themselves in a stronger position if a claim or underwriting question comes up.

1.   **Confirm rights before content goes live.** Ensure that synchronization rights, master use licenses, and any applicable blanket licenses have been secured before using music in videos posted online.

2.   **Audit existing content.** Regularly and frequently review previously published content and remove or re-license materials if rights cannot be verified. Marketing teams should have a process and procedure to follow when placing content, while always remembering that copyrighted music is rarely available to use for free.

3.   **Ensure continuous monitoring of content.** Technology can help organizations identify and remove potentially infringing content before it becomes a larger problem.

4.   **Bring legal and marketing together.** Rights review should not happen in isolation. Organizations should ensure legal and marketing teams work together when third-party content is involved.

5.   **Use contractual levers to extend policies and procedures to influencers and partners.** The same approval standards that apply internally should also apply to outside creators and brand partners.

6.   **Use outside expertise when needed.** Organizations without in-house legal resources may benefit from outside counsel or specialty licensing advisors.

7.   **Keep documentation organized.** Maintaining records of licenses, rights clearances, and agreements can make a significant difference during both claims handling and underwriting reviews.

**What this means for insurance buyers**

Coverage for music licensing and copyright claims generally sits within media liability or multimedia liability provisions of a cyber or technology errors and omissions (E&O) policy. However, carrier approaches vary considerably.

Some insurers continue to view music licensing as an exposure that can be underwritten and are willing to provide coverage when clients demonstrate strong licensing controls and remediation practices. Others have responded by introducing exclusions or revisiting policy language as claims activity increases.

Organizations should pay particular attention to older exclusionary language. Many exclusions were drafted in response to a different generation of music-related claims and may not fully reflect today's social-media-driven exposures.

That's why policy language should be reviewed carefully rather than assumed to address current risks. Because copyright claims frequently overlap with allegations involving unfair competition, false advertising, and tracking technologies, media liability and cyber coverages should be evaluated together rather than in isolation.

Music licensing and copyright litigation are no longer exposures confined to media and entertainment companies. Any organization that advertises online, publishes digital content, or works with influencers can find itself facing a claim.

The good news is that most disputes stem from preventable issues. By taking a proactive approach to licensing, monitoring, and risk management, organizations can reduce the likelihood of claims while strengthening their position with insurers.

Given the evolving nature of music licensing and copyright claims, organizations should not assume that existing practices or insurance policies adequately address today’s digital-content risks. Companies should work with their legal, marketing, and risk management teams to review licensing controls, historical content, influencer agreements, and relevant policy language. To better understand how these exposures may affect your insurance program, contact your Lockton broker to discuss available coverage options, underwriting expectations, and practical steps to strengthen your organization’s position before a claim arises.

For more cyber risk management related insights, visit:

*   Our Cyber & Technology page [here (opens a new window)](https://global.lockton.com/us/en/cyber-technology).

*   Or contact a member of Lockton’s Cyber & Technology team.

kept.heading: WHAT MAKES A GOOD LISTICLE? (6 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Freshness is the strongest ranking signal for listicles, so keep dates recent and easy for search engines to interpret. Explicit list counts also tend to perform better, with larger numbers often ranking higher. By contrast, word count, images, author bios, schema markup, and extra headings don't reliably improve rankings. Self-promotional listicles can still perform well, but putting your own product first doesn't appear to drive that growth.

Title: What makes a good listicle?

URL Source: https://www.growth-memo.com/p/what-makes-a-good-listicle

Published Time: 2026-08-31T09:10:43+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!5-vS!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4709362c-a506-4b5b-8887-88f1c26ca4d9_1672x941.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!5-vS!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4709362c-a506-4b5b-8887-88f1c26ca4d9_1672x941.png)

This Memo was sent to 28,991 subscribers. Welcome to +98 new readers! Sign up for free to get new insights every week, or sign up for Premium to get exclusive tools and frameworks that make you more effective.

How do you write a listicle that performs well in classic and AI Search?

In[last week’s Memo](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/has-google-demoted-listicles), I dug deep into 5.3M search results to see if Google demoted listicles or not.

Quick recap:

1.   **Listicles are still everywhere.** At least one true listicle appeared in the top 10 SERP results for 55.1% of the 60,000 queries analyzed, and in the top 3 for 32.3%.

2.   **Query intent is the biggest lever.** Google shows 5.3x more listicles when the query explicitly asks for a set of options.

3.   **No universal demotion.** Google shuffled who ranks: only 52.5% of queries kept the same position-one URL between January and August.

4.   **Publishers beat brands.** Publishers supplied 46.8% of the highest-ranking listicles vs. 19.2% for brands/vendors, and won 54% of head-to-head matchups on the same SERP.

5.   **Results vary sharply by vertical.** Top-10 listicle presence ranged from 42.0% (entertainment/gaming) to 67.2% (beauty/fashion); brand-owned listicles appeared on 46.2% of B2B software SERPs, reflecting how heavily B2B leans on the tactic for AI search.

6.   **The real threat is indirect: competition for attention.** 92% of listicle SERPs carried Reddit or YouTube, and AI Overviews covered 83.7% of queries on average (93.4% in B2B).

In Part 2 below, I’m answering the question: _What makes a listicle perform well?_

I analyzed over 15 variables across 3,000 listicles, but most of them didn’t survive the control checks, where I did a few analyses to determine if the findings held when normalizing certain variables. Interpret the ones with a “yes” in the _Direction stable_ column below as “maybe, but we cannot prove it yet.”

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_nCX!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2e6db242-0678-404d-b5df-ddfb783bf5d3_3600x2667.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_nCX!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2e6db242-0678-404d-b5df-ddfb783bf5d3_3600x2667.png)

**The clearest signal was freshness**. A date from the previous 2 years appeared on 66.6% of pages in the top 3, compared with 57.3% of pages in positions 8-10. That’s likely not a surprise: Search and LLMs love freshness.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mE-w!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F75011993-61e5-49d7-ad7b-40036a41bcbc_3240x4050.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mE-w!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F75011993-61e5-49d7-ad7b-40036a41bcbc_3240x4050.png)

An old date, or a date the crawler could not interpret, appeared on 8.2% of top-3 pages and 15.1% of pages in positions 8-10.

After controlling for vertical, query wording, and listicle type, an old or unreadable date was associated with **56% lower odds of ranking in the top 3** (when filtering down to one page per domain).

> If a finding from this week changes a decision for your brand, the [Growth Memo Premium Resource Library](https://library.growth-memo.com/premium) has 45+ (and growing) checklists, light tools, AI workflows, and stakeholder slide decks to put it to work.

**Counted listicles perform better.** A _counted listicle_ is one that has an explicit item count or numbered-list evidence in its title or search snippet, such as “17 Best Project Management Tools.” An _editorial roundup_ recommends or compares several options without an explicit number, such as “The Best Project Management Tools.” The name describes how the page was classified in this analysis, not whether someone manually counted every item on the page.

*   56.8% of the direct matchups went to counted listicles. This comparison covers 6,114 search results pages where a counted listicle and an editorial roundup both appeared in the organic top 10.

*   The best counted listicle averaged position 3.77 on the 28,228 search results pages where one appeared in the top 10. The best editorial roundup averaged position 4.59 across 10,791 search results pages. “Best organic rank” means the highest ordinary unpaid position reached by that page type on each search results page.

*   Counted listicles landed in the top 3 55.9% of the time when present in the top 10. Editorial roundups did so 41.4% of the time.

*   The pattern was not universal. Editorial roundups won the direct matchup in consumer technology, fitness and sports, and automotive, while counted listicles won in the other 12 verticals.

Larger title numbers rank higher. The rank pattern strengthens as the leading number in the title rises. Among explicit list queries, counted listicles with 51 to 100 in the title had a mean best organic rank of 4.11. Titles with 2 to 5 averaged position 5.85.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!aZ0R!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa30c4925-8f35-4dde-b544-9621f8eb260c_3240x4050.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!aZ0R!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa30c4925-8f35-4dde-b544-9621f8eb260c_3240x4050.png)

The leading title number is only a proxy for list length. A title can say “50 ideas” while the page contains fewer, more, or differently grouped items.

**Top-3 pages had 21.5% more words and 38.9% more images at the median**, but these differences did not remain consistent in every adjusted model. Median numbered-heading and ordered-list counts were zero in both groups.

What doesn’t help: **More section headings did not predict a better position**. A one-standard-deviation increase in heading count after adjusting for unusually large values was associated with 29% lower top-3 odds.

So, while signaling depth through big numbers in the title earns higher rankings in this dataset, over-structuring content with many headings is counterproductive.

“50 best tools” may signal comprehensiveness, match explicit list intent, or attract clicks. But 50 products can also appear in cards without creating 50 headings.

In [Part 1](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/has-google-demoted-listicles), we saw that some listicles lost traffic. In the cohort I analyzed for Part 2, I found that **self-serving listicles that were published toward the end of last year grew in traffic: 3.5x more than the rest.**

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!5MuW!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9aad6261-d1ff-406a-8469-6e76fc3909aa_3240x4050.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!5MuW!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9aad6261-d1ff-406a-8469-6e76fc3909aa_3240x4050.png)

So, while older cohorts were partially demoted by Google, newer ones travel well. However (!), **vendors putting themselves first in their listicles is not responsible for their growth**. They grow _despite_ it.

Brands aren’t publishing self-serving listicles just to rank in Google. They also want AI tools to recommend them.

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lD9E!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F16379c08-6e20-4cfd-aab5-e72ab4f6d951_900x450.png)](https://ai-visibility-index.semrush.com/downloads/chatgpt-vs-ai-mode?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=influencers&utm_campaign=socialorganic_partners_growthmemo&utm_term=social_organic&utm_content=kevinindig_august31)

Today’s sponsor, Semrush, examined how brand visibility differs between ChatGPT and Google AI Mode. Its new research analyzes 126M+ prompts across 22 industries, comparing the brands each platform mentions, the sources it cites, and the competitors it puts alongside them.

For teams publishing listicles for AI visibility, that’s useful context: the goal isn’t simply to get a page ranking, but to understand where and how your brand appears in AI answers. [Download the report for free](https://ai-visibility-index.semrush.com/downloads/chatgpt-vs-ai-mode?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=influencers&utm_campaign=socialorganic_partners_growthmemo&utm_term=social_organic&utm_content=kevinindig_august31)

After accounting for starting traffic, industry, listicle type, current rank group, and repeated pages from the same publisher, the advantage quickly disappeared. Self-promotion was associated with only 4% stronger growth, with a 95% interval ranging from 51% lower to 120% higher (p-value was 0.91).

My read is that companies put more effort into listicles after realizing their role in AI Search, and that’s why we see the growth. At the same time, the result supports the argument that self-serving listicles still work, even though Google demoted a lot of them.

> Naming your own product first holds up when the page carries something a competitor cannot copy. The [Commodity Content Audit](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/new-claude-skill-commodity-content) gives you the substitutability score before you publish, so the ranking argument rests on evidence. It’s in the [premium library](https://library.growth-memo.com/premium).

Details:

*   Across 83 manually reviewed pages from 8 industries, median organic traffic estimates reached 1,977 in August 2026 compared to 568 for 600 control listicles.

*   74.7% of eligible B2B vendor comparisons put the publisher’s own product first. 62 ranked the vendor first vs. 21 that did not.

*   Of the 434 vendor-owned B2B listicles I reviewed, 83 compared the vendor with genuine peer alternatives.

*   90.4% of self-promoting pages gained measured traffic between August 2025 and August 2026, compared with 67.3% of the overall benchmark.

*   Among pages that already had measurable traffic at the starting point, the median gain was 186%, compared with 20% for other listicles.

I get the cringe factor of writing a listicle about your brand and naming yourself first. Besides the question of whether humans would actually read this (or go to Reddit instead because they’re aware of the bias), how do you morally reconcile this?

My recommendation to clients is to use 3rd-party data as a proof point for your listicle ranking. If you have G2 reviews that support you being “the best for x”, you can write about it with a clear conscience. If not (and if you care about this), maybe listicles are not the best option. Maybe leaning on an affiliate partner or creator to do this is the better way.

There is an inherent philosophical problem with Google Search. When you search for a query like “project management software” and you’re Asana, shouldn’t you automatically show up in the search results?

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-wr9!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F560c39ce-2e33-4edc-a486-0de8613aa70d_2622x2552.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-wr9!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F560c39ce-2e33-4edc-a486-0de8613aa70d_2622x2552.png)

The answer is _no_ because there are only so many software solutions and Google doesn’t want to be “on the hook” for which brands show up first and why.

The workaround: Instead, it often links to third parties that curate brands like publishers or marketplaces. Hence, listicles. Listicles are basically curations and they avoid Google having to take a stance.

Now, AI Overviews change that. In AI Overviews, you get a clear recommendation for brands (see screenshot above). It’s a philosophical shift in how Google takes a position on which brands to recommend. And part of what allows this is personalization and longer (think: _unique_) prompts.

As a result, while listicles still rank well and might inform AI answers (perhaps less, these days), Google’s shift to name brands in AI Overviews makes their value even more questionable.

This follow-up combines four analyses from the original study of 59,984 valid Google search results pages across 60,000 US English queries and 15 verticals.

First, I compared counted listicles with editorial roundups.

*   A _counted_ _listicle_ showed an explicit item count or numbered-list evidence in its title or search snippet.

*   An _editorial roundup_ recommended several options without an explicit number.

*   Direct matchups only included search results where both formats appeared in the organic top 10.

Second, I crawled a balanced sample of 3,000 currently ranking listicles.

*   The sample contains 200 pages from each vertical, split evenly between counted listicles and editorial roundups.

The crawl recorded objective page signals, including word count, headings, estimated list items, images, author information, dates, canonical URLs, and structured data. It did not judge first-hand experience, product testing, subjective content quality, or monetization.

To identify which signals were associated with higher rankings, I compared pages whose best observed position was in the top 3 with pages in positions 8 to 10. The adjusted models accounted for vertical, query wording, listicle type, how often a page appeared in the study, and repeated pages from the same domain. I also repeated the analysis with one page per domain to limit the influence of large publishers.

Third, I compared organic traffic estimates between January 15 and a live August 24, 2026 snapshot. The sample begins with pages that ranked in August and looks backward, so it describes today’s surviving pages rather than all listicles published during the period.

Finally, I reviewed vendor-owned listicles for self-promotion. A page qualified only when it compared the vendor’s product with genuine peer alternatives. I classified it as self-promoting when the vendor placed its own product first, labeled it “Best Overall” or “Top Pick,” or otherwise made it the first substantive recommendation.

Humbly,

Kevin

PS: I gave the charts an overhaul. Would love to hear your feedback!

Title: OpenAI looks to streamline ChatGPT ad campaign creation

URL Source: https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/openai-streamlining-chatgpt-ad-campaign-creation

Published Time: 2026-08-31T11:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
OpenAI is continuing its ad platform buildout in an effort to court advertisers.

Fresh off announcing a ChatGPT ad rollout in [31 countries](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/openai-chatgpt-ads-31-new-international-markets-expansion), the AI platform is rolling out a redesigned campaign onboarding experience for advertisers launching new campaigns.

The new onboarding experience, which was detailed as part of a webinar for marketers that took place earlier this month, also included what is likely a familiar incentive for most marketers: $500 in matching ad credits for $500 in ad spend for new advertisers.

OpenAI’s pitch to advertisers comes at a pivotal time for the company. The company recently told investors its revenue grew by 18% quarter over quarter, but its losses also increased, posing challenges for the business, according to [the Wall Street Journal](https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/openais-second-quarter-sales-show-tepid-growth-compared-with-anthropic-5cb42998); the company is aiming to go public amid considerable interest in AI from investors.

As it looks for a path to profitability, OpenAI is looking for new ways to persuade marketers, who according to Emarketer are on track to spend more than [a trillion dollars](https://www.emarketer.com/content/worldwide-ad-spending-h1-2026) in 2026, to direct some of that spend to it. Central to the pitch is that ChatGPT is an attractive place to advertise as users [flock](https://www.reuters.com/technology/chatgpt-app-hits-1-billion-monthly-active-users-record-time-data-shows-2026-06-02/) to the platform with a variety of queries at various stages of intent.

“People are using [ChatGPT]to discover new products, explore their options, and ultimately decide what to buy,” Christin Klein, a global ad solutions team member who cohosted the webinar, said during the presentation. “What is different is that what was once a fragmented journey across different websites, reviews, [and] offline and online channels is now consolidated in ChatGPT. This creates a really unique opportunity for marketers.”

**How it works:** Zoheb Hajiyani, an OpenAI product team member who cohosted the webinar, said that OpenAI’s new campaign onboarding experience, redesigned to streamline campaign creation for new advertisers, can be used to construct a campaign in less than 60 seconds. According to the pitch, an advertiser can head to the website, input their website URL, and click an “Ad Preview” button, at which point OpenAI’s model will analyze the business’s objective, its product lineup, and its target customer base. The model will also suggest which user journeys on ChatGPT it may make the most sense for that advertiser’s campaign to surface.

The model then spits out an AI-generated ad, including creative and copy (that the advertiser can edit or tweak to their specifications), and will prompt the user for final details, such as where the advertiser wants to run the campaign, their bidding strategy, and billing information. Then it’s “off to the races,” Hajiyani said.

Advertisers can also build a campaign with an agent in the ChatGPT Ads Manager plug-in within ChatGPT, Hajiyani said.

“Our vision, looking forward, is to enable every business with their own intelligent performance marketer that can work alongside them inside ChatGPT and Codex—where you could simply tell your agent, ‘Hey, help me bring more customers into my restaurant. I have $500 a month to spend, and I want to spend no more than $5 per restaurant reservation,’ and that’s it. The agent could get to work.”

The new interface is set to roll out over the next few weeks, according to the company.

**Fuel to the fire:** OpenAI has been building out its ads business since rolling out its offering earlier this year, and Colin Fleming, its business CMO, recently told reporters that the company saw 25% growth in daily ad revenue since the beginning of August. The company is also rolling out its ad product internationally: Earlier this month, ChatGPT ads began running in dozens of markets, including Brazil, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, and the UK.

In July, the company published [ad credit terms](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/openai-ad-credit-policies) laying out eligibility for receiving credits and how they can be used, laying the groundwork for the credits it has begun to offer advertisers. As it continues to build out its ads business, OpenAI is also [targeting US metros](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/chatgpt-gemini-and-claude-are-expanding-their-advertising-focus-into-smaller-markets) with its own ads promoting ChatGPT, growing its ad share impressions in cities like Seattle and Boston, Marketing Brew previously reported.

Marketers across industries have been testing the channel, although many of them previously told us that they’re seeking additional [campaign controls and measurement options](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/chatgpt-advertisers-seeking-campaign-control-measurement-tools) on the channel.

kept.heading: NO AI, NO UPLOADS, NO ADS: DIVINE'S CEO SAYS FRICTION COULD SAVE SOCIAL MEDIA (5 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Divine, the app reviving Vine, bans AI content and requires videos to be filmed and verified live on-device. With no ads or algorithmic feed, it's betting that authenticity and familiar faces will matter more as AI floods social media with content.
kept.article_text:
Title: No AI, No Uploads, No Ads: Divine's CEO Says Friction Could Save Social Media

URL Source: https://www.wired.me/story/no-ai-no-uploads-no-ads-divine-ceo-says-friction-could-save-social-media

Published Time: 2026-08-31T14:25:52.581+04:00

Markdown Content:
This month, the six-second [short-form video app Vine](https://www.wired.me/story/vine-is-back-from-the-dead-and-it-brought-an-ai-bouncer) is (kind of, sort of, mostly…) back. It’s a monumental occasion for anyone who watches the platform’s old video memes in YouTube compilations, or anyone with an affinity for, say, a guy named Daniel in white vans. It’s also a pretty big moment for social media in general.

![Image 1: article image](https://media.wired.me/photos/6a8d9ec16e6325a1433166a8/master/w_775%2Cc_limit/Divine_lead.jpg)

The six-second video app’s successor is here, with archived OG content, a Taco Bell partnership and a strict human-only policy.

In recent years, the consumer internet has been hell bent on removing the friction between a person and the act of posting on a platform. Nowadays, you can upload from anywhere, anytime, edit wherever you like, duet, stitch, clip and – with varying degrees of confidence – generate with AI. You can even reach millions of strangers, let algorithms find you audiences and monetise the whole thing without leaving the app. Together, each of those decisions have produced the feeds we now trade in.

Divine, the successor to Vine which launched publicly on 18 August, is a thing built on the reversal. You cannot upload files, your FYP is deliberately detuned and AI is banned using verification tools otherwise used on war-crime footage. Creation happens inside the app or it doesn’t happen at all.

Vine was one of the buzziest digital products of the mid-2010s and housed the first real success stories of short-form video. After it was pulled offline in 2017, efforts were made to revive its digital archive, “but as an open-source project, as an internet protocol,” says Divine’s founder and CEO Evan Henshaw-Plath, who is widely referred to by his online name Rabble. The first build was a faithful reconstruction of Vine circa 2016. “Only after I announced it to the world did we see all of these old Viners want their accounts back,” he says. “All of a sudden, millions of people were asking to use it.”

![Image 2: Evan HenshawPlath commonly referred to as Rabble](https://media.wired.me/photos/6a9555df824d810e35ed052d/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/Divine_02.jpg)

Evan Henshaw-Plath, commonly referred to as Rabble

Competing video platforms are now grappling [with AI slop](https://www.wired.me/story/silicon-valley-doesnt-get-why-you-hate-ai). Divine’s approach is to cut it off at the source. “The AI ban came out of just a personal frustration,” says Henshaw-Plath. “We don’t allow uploads because we want what you see on Divine to be something you could only find on Divine. You’re not going to find reposted content from Instagram or from TikTok.”

Which also means you cannot, at least for now, produce the heavily optimised content that governs contemporary creator culture. You must pull out your phone and make something on the spot. Radical stuff. It is also a whole lot of doors to close for an app trying to build an audience in 2026, and Henshaw-Plath knows it. “Six seconds already is a massive constraint, and so is the way in which loops work,” he says. “But constraint helps art be good. It’s the reason we have rules around different kinds of poetry.”

The bet, per Henshaw-Plath, is that scarcity and friction reinstates some residual confidence in the person on the other side of the video. As much as it is a nostalgia product, Divine is also trying to be a human-first platform where the thing you’re watching could not have existed in quite the same way anywhere else.

Most Popular

As such, users can only capture raw video in real time, and the app runs Proofmode, a cryptographic verification system, to prove the footage came from a real device. “I have absolutely no plans to allow uploads,” Henshaw-Plath says. “It’s the thing that people want, but I think it will destroy what makes Divine unique.” Crucially, he doesn’t hedge that the rule might lift once the app needs to grow.

**Algorithm Game**

Vine was in its prime before social media was so [algorithmically driven](https://www.wired.me/story/this-social-media-ceo-is-sick-of-the-algorithm). Back then, at least, you were fed those you followed, and Henshaw-Plath wants to reissue the sense of community that formed around natural repeated interaction. Divine has a “For You” feed, detuned on the theory that unrestrained recommendation dissolves the relationship between a creator and the same faces returning each week. “A creator doesn’t tend to talk to the same audience over and over again, because every video is mostly shown to new people,” Henshaw-Plath says, “but that’s not the Vine experience."

![Image 3: article image](https://media.wired.me/photos/6a4df8a5ccd4c130ffaa8e28/master/w_775%2Cc_limit/Upscrolled_lead1.jpg)

Upscrolled’s founder Issam Hijazi says algorithms were built to make you addicted to social media platforms. Now he’s trying to build one without them.

The in-app editing toolset follows the same doctrine, offering green screen, lip sync and stop motion as “non-AI ways of helping people edit and produce stuff in the camera app.” Though Square uploads were Vine’s domain, Divine permits a vertical aspect ratio too, and claims the current usage of both formats splits roughly evenly.

Most Popular

For the creators themselves, the constraints of the app will likely mean it isn’t for everyone, claims Henshaw-Plath. But it was never meant to be a platform through which all content would pass. “I don’t think we need social media apps to be a winner-take-all world in which a single app rules them all,” he says. “In fact, if we have a world in which a single app dominates everything, then something is really wrong, because that is a world in which we get monocultures.”

Vine birthed some of the first large-scale short-form content creators, some of which have already reclaimed their accounts. Yet Divine is refusing, for now at least, to rebuild the platform-controlled creator economy. “We don’t have all the monetisation stuff figured out. We don’t even have the plan figured out, but we do know that it needs to be a reset where Divine isn’t owning and controlling all the power,” Henshaw-Plath says.

He argues that paying creators to post is not a healthy relationship, but insists they can use links, tips and payment handles from whichever providers they choose, and thus take brand partnerships on the platform directly. As of now, there are no plans for in-app advertising either. “I don’t want to build a home shopping network,” he adds. “It’s fine that it exists. It’s just not what I want.”

The new platform is, then, one big accumulation of refusals. With no AI, no uploads, no ads and no storefront, the wager underneath is that friction is not a tax on the experience but the sell itself. And that an internet that is drowning in synthetic slop will eventually pay a hefty premium for sheer proof of human creation. It is a pretty defensible bet about culture. Time will tell if it is a bet that’ll pay off.

Title: Google AI Overviews Pushing Searchers Into AI Mode, Drops Show More Button

URL Source: https://www.seroundtable.com/google-ai-overviews-push-ai-mode-responses-41974.html

Published Time: 2026-08-28T13:30:00-04:00

Markdown Content:
[Home](https://www.seroundtable.com/) / [Google News](https://www.seroundtable.com/category/google) / [Google AI Overviews Pushing Searchers Into AI Mode, Drops Show More Button](https://www.seroundtable.com/google-ai-overviews-push-ai-mode-responses-41974.html)

![Image 1: Google Confetti](https://images.seroundtable.com/google-confetti-LdTG0ArZ.jpg)

Google Search has confirmed it is now pushing searchers into AI Mode from the AI Overview by default, without having to click the "Show more" button. The new AI Overview experience that Google is testing shows a much fuller AI answer, like you'd get in AI Mode, and loads the follow up "Ask anything" box by default.

This pushes the default search results, the ten blue links, way down lower on the page. "For some queries, AI Overviews may dynamically expand for topics where our systems determine it’s most useful for people," a Google spokesperson told us.

I am able to replicate this, but it was first spotted by Chris Long who posted an example of this on [X](https://x.com/chris_nectiv/status/2092984357782794593) - he wrote, "Holy moly SEOs: Google is now revealing the AI Mode prompt box BY DEFAULT for some queries." "This is how Google continues to push AI Mode as the default search experience," he added.

Here is a GIF I made of this:

![Image 2: Google Ai Overview No Show More](https://images.seroundtable.com/google-ai-overview-no-show-more-Clm4zUw7.gif)

To understand the difference between how AI Overviews used to work, Google would load a snippet of the AI Overview, and you'd have to click "Show more" to see the full AI Overview response.

Like this:

[![Image 3: Google Ai Overview Show More Button](https://images.seroundtable.com/google-ai-overview-show-more-button-mfyfhXJe.png)](https://images.seroundtable.com/google-ai-overview-show-more-button-mfyfhXJe.png)

But for some queries, it just loads the full AI Overview, with the Ask anything box already opened. Pushing down the organic search results way below the AI Answer:

[![Image 4: Google Ai Overview No Show More](https://images.seroundtable.com/google-ai-overview-no-show-more-UpK8bqH2.png)](https://images.seroundtable.com/google-ai-overview-no-show-more-UpK8bqH2.png)

Here is the post from Chris:

> Holy moly SEOs: Google is now revealing the AI Mode prompt box BY DEFAULT for some queries.
> 
> 
> This is how Google continues to push AI Mode as the default search experience. [pic.twitter.com/Ero2pj3BZf](https://t.co/Ero2pj3BZf)
> 
> — Chris Long (@chris_nectiv) [August 27, 2026](https://x.com/chris_nectiv/status/2092984357782794593?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

This is not good for publishers, not good at all. But I think we all expected this to happen.

A Google spokesperson sent us the following statement:

> "For some queries, AI Overviews may dynamically expand for topics where our systems determine it’s most useful for people. Our research has shown that with this dynamic experience, users find Search more helpful and engage deeper in follow-up exploration."

I should note that if a user has already begun scrolling to view content below the AI Overview, Google cancels the expansion to prevent the user from losing their reading position.

Forum discussion at [X](https://x.com/chris_nectiv/status/2092984357782794593).

Update: Robby Stein from Google also responded about this:

> Hey Barry, jumping in here with more context, AI Overviews only dynamically expand for topics where our systems determine it to be most useful. If you’ve already started scrolling, the expansion stops to keep your place.
> 
> 
> We're always testing and tuning these experiences, so…
> 
> — Robby Stein (@rmstein) [August 28, 2026](https://x.com/rmstein/status/2093446202385956896?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Copied!

[The Exchange](https://www.cnbc.com/the-exchange/)

The Federal Trade Commission on Monday sued [Amazon](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/AMZN/), alleging the e-commerce giant “secretly and systematically overcharged” advertisers on its platform by manipulating its pricing and auction systems.

The [lawsuit](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/08/ftc-states-sue-amazon-over-secret-ad-surcharge-scheme), which was joined by 22 state attorneys general, argues that Amazon may have reaped more than $20 billion from advertisers by using “hidden surcharges” dating back to a change to its auction rules that took effect in 2019.

“Amazon has millions of advertising customers who were misled into paying significantly higher prices,” FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said in a statement. “These higher costs were largely passed on to American consumers.”

In [a blog post](https://www.aboutamazon.com/company-news/amazon-ftc-sponsored-ads-lawsuit-response?utm_source=rss), Amazon called the FTC’s lawsuit “misguided” and said the complaint “fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate.” The company added that the agency’s lawsuit doesn’t include evidence of consumer price increases.

“We’ve provided advertisers with guidance about our auctions and pricing in the main tools they use to manage their campaigns, and we continue to update that guidance,” the company said. “We look forward to making our case in court.”

The company said its auction systems have saved advertisers $8 billion between 2021 and 2025, not cost them extra.

The complaint, which was filed in U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington, centers on Amazon’s sponsored products ads, brands ads and display ads that run alongside search results on its sprawling webstore.

Amazon has amassed the third-largest digital advertising business globally, trailing only [Google](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/GOOGL/) and [Meta](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/META/). The company hauled in more than [$68 billion](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1018724/000101872426000004/amzn-20251231.htm) in ads revenue last year, with the lion’s share coming from sales of sponsored products ads.

[Third-party sellers](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/04/15/amazon-sellers-boycott-ads-payment-changes.html) who hawk their wares on Amazon’s marketplace have recently criticized surging advertising costs on the site, including a string of recent policy changes, which led to some top merchants withholding their ad spend in a boycott.

The company has traditionally used a “second-price” auction system, wherein it told advertisers they “only pay the least bid amount needed in order to win,” the complaint states, citing Amazon’s own marketing materials.

The FTC alleges in its complaint that Amazon in 2019 changed its auction rules without notice by adding an undisclosed surcharge it referred to as a “soft reserve price,” which led to higher ad prices.

“Amazon made this surreptitious change to its auction because it was unhappy about how much revenue its advertising auctions were generating,” the agency said in its complaint, which cites internal communications between Amazon ad executives.

In one exchange, a company executive allegedly acknowledged it uses an “invented auction participant” to increase prices, the FTC said.

The FTC and the states alleged Amazon’s practices violate federal and state consumer protection laws, and they’re seeking civil penalties, restitution and other unspecified damages.

It marks the latest example of Amazon being caught in the FTC’s crosshairs. Last September, Amazon reached a [$2.5 billion settlement](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/09/25/amazon-ftc-prime-settlement.html) with the agency to resolve a separate probe into its Prime membership program.

The company is also expected to head to trial next year in a case brought by the [FTC and 17 states](https://www.cnbc.com/2023/09/26/ftc-and-17-states-sue-amazon-on-antitrust-charges.html) that accuses it of wielding its “monopoly power” to inflate prices, squash third-party sellers and degrade quality for shoppers. Amazon has denied any wrongdoing.

Title: How We’d Market a $400 Skincare Device Before Black Friday

URL Source: https://sparktoro.com/blog/how-wed-market-a-400-skincare-device-before-black-friday/

Published Time: 2026-08-26T04:19:38+00:00

Markdown Content:
I’ve been trying to streamline my skincare routine while still getting solid results. The 10-step Korean skincare routine? It’s lovely, but I no longer have the patience to fit that into my schedule… or into my budget. So I started on a tretinoin prescription, Vanicream Daily Facial Moisturizer twice a day, Medik8 C-Tetra Vitamin C serum in the morning, and Skinfix Triple Lipid-Peptide Cream at night. That’s it.

Oh, and my $400 [CurrentBody LED face mask](https://www.currentbody.us/products/currentbody-skin-led-light-therapy-mask). Not even to humble-brag, but brag-brag, I look really cool wearing it.

![Image 1](https://images.sparktoro.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Amanda_LEDFaceMask-1024x576.jpg)

I know the text in this thumbnail isn’t really the point of this post, but how else am I gonna get people to read this?! Also, I do answer this question, so keep reading…

So naturally, I decided to build CurrentBody’s Black Friday Cyber Monday marketing strategy. It’s almost September, so we better get a move on!

CurrentBody’s Series 2 LED face mask currently sells for $469.99 in the U.S., putting it firmly in “I’m going to think about this purchase for a minute” territory. It’s not a $14 sheet mask you toss into your Sephora cart because the packaging was compelling. It’s a beauty device you’re likely to research, compare, rationalize, abandon in your cart, reconsider, watch three YouTube reviews about, and perhaps finally buy when Black Friday gives you permission.

Which makes it an excellent audience research problem.

For this [Audience Research Brief](https://sparktoro.com/blog/category/audience-research-briefs/), I ran a SparkToro report on:

Women in the U.S. seeking at-home LED anti-aging treatments. SparkToro estimates that audience at just over 1 million people, with an estimated market value of $44.9-$56.7 billion.

![Image 2](https://images.sparktoro.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-25-at-7.55.10-PM-1024x510.png)
My question was simple:

_If CurrentBody wants to sell a bunch of LED masks during Black Friday/Cyber Monday, what should it be doing before Black Friday arrives?_

Because my suspicion is that for a considered purchase like this one, the most important part of your Black Friday marketing happens before the sale. And the audience research supports that.

First: do these LED masks actually do anything?

**Important detour!**

I am a skincare enthusiast, not a dermatologist. I do not believe my glowing red Hannibal Lecter mask is the fountain of youth. But red-light therapy is also not pure TikTok woo.

The [American Academy of Dermatology says](https://www.aad.org/public/cosmetic/safety/red-light-therapy) research suggests red-light LED devices can produce “subtle to noticeable” improvements in fine lines and wrinkles, discoloration, roughness, and loose skin, while also cautioning that at-home devices vary and that more research is needed to determine optimal treatment protocols.

There are randomized trials behind the category, too. In [one 2023 randomized trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36780572/) of 137 women ages 40-65, ten sessions of red or amber photobiomodulation over four weeks produced about a 30% reduction in measured wrinkle volume around the eyes. The treatments did not significantly improve every measure studied, including hydration and elasticity — a useful reminder that “supported by evidence” and “magic face time machine” are very different claims.

So, there is legitimate science here. But there are also plenty of reasons for a $470 shopper to have questions.

Which brings us back to the marketing.

## Insight #1: This audience uses social media. They just don’t over-index on it.

Here’s something I would have guessed incorrectly. If you asked me where women interested in anti-aging skincare devices spend their time, I’d reflexively say Instagram. TikTok. Pinterest. YouTube.

And yes! They use all of those places.

According to our report, 87.9% of this audience uses YouTube monthly. About 76% use Facebook, 75% Instagram, 75% Reddit, and 56% TikTok.

![Image 3](https://images.sparktoro.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/overview-data-networks-graph-women-seeking-at-home-led-anti-aging-treatments-1-1024x588.png)
But compared with the average U.S. web user, this audience under-indexes on every one of those platforms. YouTube is about 8% below average. Facebook 12%. Instagram 5%. Reddit 7%. TikTok 13%. LinkedIn, X, and Pinterest are even further below their respective U.S. averages.

That does not mean CurrentBody should pump the brakes on social media. After all, 75% audience reach on Instagram is… 75% audience reach!

This is where marketers can get tripped up by affinity data. Reach tells you whether a channel matters. Indexing tells you whether this audience is unusually concentrated there.

Instagram could absolutely belong in the media plan. But the data doesn’t support the lazy version of the strategy: Beauty product → beauty influencer → Instagram → done.

Next up: this audience’s information diet gets much more interesting when we look beyond social.

## Insight #2: Apparently the LED-mask girlies are on Claude?!

About 37% of this audience uses ChatGPT monthly, only slightly above the U.S. average. **But Claude? 16.9% of this audience uses Claude, versus about 5.3% of the U.S. web population.** That’s a 221% over-index.

![Image 4](https://images.sparktoro.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-25-at-8.09.15-PM-1024x575.png)
Gemini also slightly over-indexes, while most of the broader AI category does not. In fact, AI and machine-learning websites as a category account for a smaller share of this audience’s browsing than they do for the average web user.

Their AI usage is selective — and Claude is unusually prevalent among them.

The practical implication is bigger than “optimize for Claude.”

It means AI answers plausibly belong somewhere in this buyer’s research journey. And when we look at what this audience is actually prompting and searching for, that journey becomes a lot clearer.

## Insight #3: These people are doing their homework.

The highest-affinity search terms include:

*   “led face mask”
*   “best led face mask”
*   “best led mask for wrinkles”
*   “red light mask benefits”
*   “led face mask reviews”
*   “led face mask before and after”
*   “led face mask results”
*   “how often use led mask”
*   “led mask skincare routine”

And the AI prompt topics tell almost exactly the same story: LED mask reviews, results, safety, comparisons, cost, dermatologist recommendations, wavelength differences, CurrentBody, Omnilux, and more.

That is a consideration-stage audience if I ever saw one. They’re asking thoughtful, high-intent questions like:

*   Does this stuff work?
*   Which one works best?
*   Is it safe?
*   How long until I see results?
*   What’s the difference between red and near-infrared light?
*   What do dermatologists recommend?
*   CurrentBody or Omnilux?
*   Is this thing worth several hundred dollars?

Those are very different marketing problems from “How do we make someone aware that CurrentBody exists?”

And they’re exactly the kinds of questions I’d want CurrentBody answering months before the Black Friday promo drops. Because by November, this shopper needs enough evidence to decide which mask deserves her money.

## Insight #4: Beauty credibility here comes from a fascinating mix of editorial, clinical, and community sources.

Look at the websites this audience prefers:

Allure. NewBeauty. Dermstore. Paula’s Choice. Soko Glam. Ulta. Then come RealSelf, Obagi, ZO Skin Health, Omnilux, the American Academy of Dermatology, Skin Cancer Foundation, Health.com, mindbodygreen, Well+Good, and more.

That’s a fascinating information ecosystem. It isn’t purely aspirational beauty media, or purely clinical. It’s a mix of beauty, evidence, reviews, and expertise. You can see the same pattern on YouTube. CurrentBody itself has the highest affinity, followed by FiftyPlusBeauty, skincare-review channels, and the American Academy of Dermatology.

Podcasts lean heavily toward skin science, aesthetics, anti-aging, dermatology, and healthy aging: Biohacking Beauty, Spa Skin and Beauty, Aged to Perfection, and Bathroom Diaries with Dr. Sofia Din are among the highest-affinity shows.

And then there’s Reddit. The audience as a whole actually under-indexes somewhat on Reddit compared with the U.S. average.

But look at the communities:

r/SkincareAddiction: 99/100 affinity

r/30PlusSkinCare: 98/100

r/redlighttherapy: 98/100

r/AsianBeauty: 93/100

r/beauty: 91/100

If I’m on the CurrentBody marketing or heck, product team, I’d use those communities as research infrastructure. What questions keep appearing? What objections? What comparisons? What kinds of evidence make people skeptical? Which products get recommended organically? What makes somebody say, “Fine. Take my money.”

## Insight #5: CurrentBody already has brand affinity. But the audience’s attention lives all over the place.

CurrentBody ranks #1 for brand affinity, at 98/100. Omnilux comes next at 97, followed by Dr. Dennis Gross at 94. Allure, Obagi, ZO Skin Health, Dermstore, RealSelf, NewBeauty, and Paula’s Choice are also among the brands with the strongest affinity. CurrentBody clearly has meaningful relevance with this audience.

But look at where the audience spends its web attention.

![Image 5](https://images.sparktoro.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/websites-women-seeking-at-home-led-anti-aging-treatments-1024x907.png)
CurrentBody.com sits below Allure, NewBeauty, Dermstore, Paula’s Choice, Soko Glam, Ulta, SkinStore, Beautylish, Lookfantastic, The Ordinary, RealSelf, mindbodygreen, Omnilux, Well+Good, and several others in the website-affinity rankings.

It illustrates a very real truth that almost certainly applies to ecommerce, generally. The audience doesn’t conduct its entire buying journey on your website. People form opinions elsewhere. They learn from Allure. They browse Dermstore. They read NewBeauty. They ask Reddit. They watch YouTube. They search Google. They apparently ask Claude! They compare you with Omnilux. And then, perhaps, they visit your website — when they’re ready to swipe that credit card.

![Image 6](https://images.sparktoro.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/audience-visits-women-seeking-at-home-led-anti-aging-treatments-1024x556.png)
This is the Zero Click Marketing problem in the microcosm of one brand. The marketing job isn’t merely getting everyone onto CurrentBody.com. It’s getting CurrentBody into the places where people learn what to trust before they’re ready to buy.

## What we’d actually do before Black Friday

If I were building CurrentBody’s BFCM plan from this research, I would work backwards from November.

### August-September: Win the research phase

I’d build or refresh the best possible resources answering the questions this audience already asks:

How does red-light therapy work? What evidence supports it? What wavelengths matter? How long until results appear? CurrentBody vs. competitors: what are the actual differences? Who shouldn’t use an LED mask? How does it fit into a skincare routine?

Some of that content should live on CurrentBody’s own site. But I’d care just as much about getting those answers distributed and cited elsewhere.

Pitch editors at the beauty publications this audience trusts. Give independent reviewers useful products and good information without trying to control their verdict. Put credible experts in a position to explain the technology. Make comparison information easy for search engines and AI systems to retrieve and understand.

### September-October: Borrow trust

I’d look hard at Allure, The Cut, NewBeauty, relevant skincare YouTubers, dermatologists, aesthetic professionals, podcasts, Dermstore, and the other high-affinity sources in the report, and I’d think about how I could tap into the trust their audience has in them. Content like a dermatologist explaining what consumers should look for in an LED mask can create category demand, or an Allure article explaining red-light therapy can move somebody toward purchase even if CurrentBody only gets one paragraph.

Influence doesn’t require ownership of the interaction.

### October-early November: Help people choose

Now I’d turn harder toward comparison-oriented content.

*   CurrentBody vs. Omnilux.
*   What makes one LED mask different from another?
*   Does wavelength matter?
*   How often do you need to use it?
*   What does the evidence actually show?
*   What’s worth paying extra for?

This is also where I’d be checking search results, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Reddit, YouTube, and editorial coverage for category questions. When somebody asks, “What’s the best LED mask for wrinkles?” does CurrentBody appear in the answer? More importantly: why?

What sources are informing that recommendation? Are we present in those sources?

## Black Friday: Finally, sell the dang mask

Paid social. Search ads. Retargeting. Email. Affiliates. Creators. Whatever promotional mechanics make financial sense. This audience still has enormous absolute usage of YouTube, Instagram, Facebook, Reddit and TikTok even when those platforms under-index. At this point in the strategy, paid marketing efforts should have a much easier job because it will have arrived after three months of familiarity and evidence.

Instead of asking one Black Friday ad to introduce the brand, explain LED therapy, convince someone it isn’t snake oil (there’s a skincare-related pun in here I’m sure, but I am tired), differentiate the mask from competitors, justify the price tag, AND create urgency… I would let August, September, and October do most of that work.

Then November gets to swoop in with an easier conversion job, “Hey. I see you, boo. You know that thing you’ve been considering? It’s on sale.”

## The bigger lesson for marketers

CurrentBody is just our example. The same principle applies to any considered purchase.

If you’re selling a $2,000 mattress, a $5,000 piece of software, a new car, an expensive appliance, or yes, a face mask that makes its wearer look like a glamorous cybercriminal, your customer’s decision probably starts long before your promotional window.

Audience research helps you see that invisible part of the journey, and now that it’s (*checks calendar*) already the end of August, that journey has already started. Because if Black Friday is the moment your customer first encounters you, you may already be late.

[**Create your next Audience Research Report in SparkToro** and](https://sparktoro.com/) start mapping out your next big marketing strategy.

And CurrentBody? If you’re reading this, I wouldn’t hate it if you sent me some additional products.

kept.heading: THE PAGES YOUR AGENCY BUILT TO WIN AI CITATIONS JUST LOST HALF OF THEM (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: ChatGPT and Google are reducing visibility for the listicles and comparison pages that have powered many agency AI visibility programs since 2024. ChatGPT citations for listicles fell 50.5%, from 15.77% to 7.80%, after its August 6 update, while product pages rose to 16.39% of retrieved pages. Brands should audit citation performance by page type and invest more in primary product and pricing pages that provide specifications and real information directly on the vendor's domain. AI visibility now favors useful source material over pages built mainly to match "best," "top," or "vs" queries.

# The Pages Your Agency Built to Win AI Citations Just Lost Half of Them

August 31, 2026

ChatGPT halved its listicle citations on August 6 and Google demoted the same kind of page twelve days later. Roundups and comparison articles have been the core deliverable in AI visibility retainers since 2024.

## Make State of Brand one of your go-to sources on Google

[![Image 13: Google Icon](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/69d5f4156c1e2de2879d2837/6a13c9bfa24746699092f7de_Google_Favicon_2025.svg%201.avif) Add State of Brand on Google](https://ter.li/6uh2y55q)

OpenAI moved Free and Go accounts onto GPT-5.6 Luna on August 6 and [retuned the model serving Plus and Pro](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-5-6-august-update) the same day, adding a slider that lets paid users choose how much effort ChatGPT puts into a response. [Peec AI ran its citation numbers that day](https://lilyraynyc.substack.com/p/what-we-can-learn-from-evolving-chatgpt). Listicles fell from 15.77% of ChatGPT's citations to 7.80%, a relative drop of 50.5%. [Comparison pages fell from 9.08% to 6.17%](https://x.com/lilyraynyc/status/2090256147441746150), down 32.1%.

The fan-out queries went with them. Those are the searches ChatGPT fires off behind the scenes before it writes an answer, and [the ones containing "best," "top," "vs," and "comparison"](https://x.com/lilyraynyc/status/2090256147441746150) now make up a smaller share of the total. Fewer queries of that shape means fewer chances for a page built around that shape to get pulled in.

Product pages picked up the slack. [They now account for 16.39% of retrieved pages](https://lilyraynyc.substack.com/p/what-we-can-learn-from-evolving-chatgpt), which puts them ahead of listicles. Asked about a category, the model has become more likely to go to the manufacturer for specifications and pricing than to a roundup written by a site earning commission on the products inside it.

ChatGPT is also doing more work per answer and crediting fewer sources for it. [Prompts resolved with a single fan-out query dropped from 94.0% to 43.5%](https://lilyraynyc.substack.com/p/what-we-can-learn-from-evolving-chatgpt), and the average number of retrieved sources roughly doubled, from about twelve to about twenty-four. Olivier de Segonzac and the team at Resoneo, working separately, [found unique domains cited per response falling from 19 to 15](https://lilyraynyc.substack.com/p/what-we-can-learn-from-evolving-chatgpt) after an earlier update, which points the same way from the other end.

## Google moved twelve days later

Google started rolling out [its third spam update of the year](https://modo25.com/blog/seo/googles-august-spam-update-how-to-avoid-scaled-content-abuse/) on August 18 and finished on the 21st, [two days and sixteen hours later](https://www.savvydealer.com/blog/google-august-2026-spam-update-dealer-scaled-content), across every language and location. The company called it routine, announced no new policies, and published nothing about it beyond a line in its ranking updates history.

What sits behind it happened in May. On the 15th, [Google rewrote the opening line of its search spam policies](https://modo25.com/blog/seo/googles-august-spam-update-how-to-avoid-scaled-content-abuse/) so that the definition now covers attempts to manipulate generative AI responses in Google Search. Scaled content abuse, which [describes pages produced in volume mainly to move rankings](https://www.savvydealer.com/blog/google-august-2026-spam-update-dealer-scaled-content) and names generative AI tools among the ways it happens, has been policy since 2024. The May edit stretched that policy from ranking to getting cited, and the August update is the first serious enforcement pass since it landed.

Blue-link ranking and AI Overview citation run on separate retrieval systems, and nobody is suggesting the two companies coordinated. Two systems that share nothing operationally moved against the same content format inside a fortnight. That says something about how much of it there is and how visible it had become to both of them.

## What the retainer bought

AI visibility work sold since 2024 has been consistent in what it produces. Category roundups. "Best [category] software 2026." Head-to-head comparison pages, often naming competitors the company would never mention anywhere else. Alternatives pages. Published on a schedule, at volume, usually by an agency, usually on a line item labeled GEO or AEO.

Those pages worked, which is why so many of them exist. They were cheap to produce using the same models now declining to cite them, they were the highest-leverage format available at the time, and for roughly eighteen months they returned. Nobody bought them out of foolishness.

They are losing ground on both surfaces at once, and the reason is structural. A page that exists only to catch a comparison query has no audience underneath it. When retrieval behavior shifts, nothing holds it up.

## What to do about it this week

Pull your own citation data and split it by page type, comparing July against the back half of August. Most AI visibility tools report aggregate mentions, and aggregate mentions cannot show you this.

Work out what share of everything you published in the last year was roundup or comparison format, and how much of that came from a vendor. Call the vendor and ask what they are telling clients about the August data. The quality of that answer is worth more than the deck they sent you in January.

Then look at your product and pricing pages, because that is where the retrieval is going. We have [written before](https://www.thestateofbrand.com/news/great-flattening-ai-search-invisible-brands) that most of what ChatGPT cites does not rank on Google. The Peec numbers add something to it. The model wants primary sources, in plain HTML, on the vendor's own domain, with real specifications and real prices on the page. B2B has spent ten years moving exactly that information behind a form.

The cheap version of this had a good run. What replaces it will cost more, because a page that earns a citation on the merits takes longer to write than a page shaped like the query it was built to catch.

kept.heading: THE STORE ISN'T DEAD—BUT THE MERCHANT MODEL IS (8 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: More than 7,300 US stores closed last year, the most since 2020, while store openings held just as strong, evidence that retail formats are evolving rather than physical stores disappearing. The actual weak point is the merchant model, which has retailers forecasting demand and owning inventory months before they know if it will sell. A growing number of retailers are shifting to a store-in-store setup instead, renting curated space to brands that carry their own inventory risk, the way Harrods lets luxury labels run their own sections and set their own prices. AI shopping agents are pushing the shift further, since faster demand swings raise the cost of the merchant model's forecasting bets.
