Title: The Store Isn’t Dead—but the Merchant Model Is

URL Source: https://hbr.org/2026/08/the-store-isnt-dead-but-the-merchant-model-is

Published Time: 2026-08-31T12:15:12.000+00:00

Markdown Content:
Walk through a department store at the end of a season and the signs tell a familiar story: 40% off! 60% off! Clearance! Retailers often treat these markdowns as a tactical problem, the result of the wrong product, the wrong promotion, or bad weather effects. But they are better understood as confessions. They reveal the downsides of the traditional retailing model. The retailer acted as a merchant, committed to inventory before demand was known, absorbed the risk of being wrong, and then paid for that error in margin erosion and brand equity dilution. Under this merchant model, retailers routinely take on more risk than they can handle.

Store-closing numbers tell the same story on a larger scale. Coresight Research tracked [7,325 U.S. store closures in 2024](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250123760119/en/Coresight-Research-Predicts-2025-Store-Opening-Closure-Numbers), the highest total since 2020, [when closures approached 10,000](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250123760119/en/Coresight-Research-Predicts-2025-Store-Opening-Closure-Numbers). JLL reported that announced closures between 2024 and early 2025 [totaled more than 9,900 locations](https://www.jll.com/content/dam/jllcom/en/us/documents/reports/research-reports/25-research-us-retail-market-dynamics-q1-2025.pdf).

It is tempting to read these numbers as proof that the store is dying. That is the wrong conclusion. Store openings have also [remained substantial](https://www.jll.com/content/dam/jllcom/en/us/documents/reports/research-reports/25-research-us-retail-market-dynamics-q1-2025.pdf), and much vacated space is being backfilled by stronger concepts. The evidence points not to consumer flight from stores, but to an evolution of retail models. Stores that offer the right combination of convenience, value, service, experience, or access to distinctive brands can still thrive, but that combination is always changing. Stores built around the static merchant model are under pressure because they carry too much inventory risk in a market where demand has become harder to predict.

This is not a new cycle. Stanley Hollander’s classic [wheel of retailing](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/002224296002500106), first published in 1960, described how retail formats often enter as lean, low-margin, low-price challengers, then gradually trade up—better locations, more services, higher costs, higher margins—and eventually become vulnerable to the next low-cost entrant. That wheel continues to turn. Department stores, malls, discount stores, category killers, big-box retailers, and e-commerce platforms have all taken their turns.

The urgent question for retailers is whether they must keep riding the wheel. We believe they should not.

To break out of the wheel of retailing, retailers must stop treating each new format as a better way to merchandise goods and start treating retail as a platform for allocating risk. The problem is not physical retail. The problem is a model that asks retailers to buy inventory far in advance, forecast across thousands of stock keeping units (SKUs), absorb the cost of error, and then train customers to wait for markdowns.

In a slower, less fragmented market, the risks created by the merchant model were more manageable. Today they are punishing. Consumer preferences shift faster. Brand cycles are shorter. Social media can create and destroy demand in days. Omnichannel operations multiply complexity. The old merchant model forces retailers to make bigger bets with less reliable information.

Better analytics help. So do faster replenishment systems, AI forecasting, and demand sensing. But they do not solve the structural issue: The party making the inventory decision is often not the party closest to product-level demand, and neither is it the party incentivized properly to do the best for a product.

There are two broad ways to reduce mismatch between supply and demand.

The first is to delay commitment by ordering in small quantities, observing demand, and then making more substantial buy orders. This requires real time demand analytics and the ability to source more locally.

The second is to move the decision to the entity with better product knowledge. Brand owners often understand their categories, assortments, price ladders, and customer signals better than a retailer’s centralized buying organization can. A merchant may be responsible for dozens of brands and hundreds or thousands of SKUs. A brand is focused on its own line, its own customers, and its own demand signals. The question is not whether retailers should give up judgment. It is whether they should stop assuming that centralized buying is always the best place for demand risk to sit.

That is why [the store-in-store model](https://www.jstor.org/stable/20751538?seq=1) deserves far more attention than it receives in the United States. In a store-in-store arrangement, the retailer provides traffic, location, environment, and customer access. The brand operates its own space, often with control over assortment, inventory, service, presentation, and pricing. The retailer becomes less of a merchant and more of a platform.

A poster child for store-in-store is [Harrods](https://www.harrods.com/en-us) of London, which promotes a partnership model with worldwide brands. Managing Director [Michael Ward](https://www.worldretailcongress.com/speakers/michael-ward) sees this as a competitive advantage. Brands are welcome to take ownership of their own space at Harrods and to curate and forecast for their own SKUs.

Our [research](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1509/jmkr.47.4.748) and interviews on store-in-store models show why this structure can work. By giving manufacturers autonomy inside the retailer’s space, the retailer can improve channel efficiency and service quality, while charging for access to valuable customer traffic. The manufacturer can get quick feedback from the market and avail itself of the full control over its distribution channel in the way that Apple does, but without owning any of its stores. The arrangement is especially powerful when in-store service matters and when brands are not simple substitutes for one another. The irony is that a powerful retailer may create more value by giving up some control.

Online retail has already moved in this direction. Marketplaces such as Amazon and Alibaba do not simply buy and resell every product. They often let sellers reach customers directly, charging fees for access to traffic, data, logistics, or platform services. [Research](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/mnsc.2015.2230) on agency selling in electronic retailing makes the same strategic point: agency models can be more efficient than conventional reselling, although the platform gives up some price control. The platform wins not by owning every product decision, but by designing the rules of participation.

Offline retailers can learn from this. A department store does not need to be a warehouse with nicer lighting. It can be a physical marketplace: a curated, governed platform where brands bear more inventory risk and retailers concentrate on traffic, trust, experience, and portfolio design.

This also changes how we should think about retail buyers—the professionals who decide what goes on store shelves. In the traditional model, buyers are powerful intermediaries. They decide what to order, how much to order, and which manufacturers get floor space. But [research](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/full/10.1287/mnsc.2021.01646) on retail buyers and manufacturer influence shows that this role is [vulnerable to distorted incentives](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/mnsc.2021.01646). Manufacturers may try to influence buyers through gifts, entertainment, travel, or other inducements. The deeper issue is not simply misconduct. It is that the buying function becomes a contested bottleneck where manufacturers and retailers both try to shape the buyer’s demand assessment.

Better compensation and governance can reduce these distortions. But the larger lesson is structural: When too much demand judgment is concentrated in a buyer who is not closest to the end consumer or the product category, the system invites error and influence. Platform-based retailing does not eliminate governance needs. It changes them. The retailer still decides which brands belong on the platform, what standards they must meet, how customer data are shared, and how conflicts are resolved. But it reduces the need for the retailer to make every SKU-level inventory bet.

This is not a call for retailers to rent out space indiscriminately. A weak platform becomes a bazaar. A strong platform has rules. It curates brands carefully, protects the customer experience, manages adjacency, sets service standards, and removes partners that undermine the proposition. The retailer’s role becomes more strategic, not less.

In many European and Asian department stores, branded spaces are not side experiments; they are central to the operating model. Brands curate their own areas and assume more responsibility for demand, inventory, staffing, presentation and pricing. The retailer orchestrates the overall symphony.

The United States has examples too, though often as partial experiments. [Beauty counters](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1509/jmkr.47.4.748) have long operated this way. Macy’s has [partnered with](https://www.macysinc.com/newsroom/news/news-details/2022/Macys-Inc.-Insider-Elevating-the-Toy-Store-Experience-Through-Our-ToysRUs-Partnership-10-24-2022/default.aspx) Toys“R”Us. Kohl’s has built a [major relationship](https://investors.kohls.com/news/news-details/2022/Kohls-and-Sephora-Announce-Planned-Expansion-of-Sephora-Presence-to-All-Kohls-Stores/default.aspx) with Sephora. Target has experimented with [Disney](https://corporate.target.com/press/release/2019/10/disney-store-at-target-shop-in-shop-launches-onlin), [Apple](https://corporate.target.com/press/release/2022/10/target-and-apple-deepen-collaboration-with-more-sh), [CVS](https://corporate.target.com/press/release/2015/06/cvs-health-and-target-sign-agreement-for-cvs-health-to-acquire%2C-rebrand-and-operate-target-s-pharma), [Starbucks](https://corporate.target.com/press/fact-sheet/2022/11/about-target-drive-up-with-starbucks%2C-our-new-fulfillment-feature), [Warby Parker](https://corporate.target.com/press/release/2025/02/target-and-warby-parker-team-up-to-bring-stylish%2C-affordable-eyewear-to-more-consumers), and [Ulta](https://corporate.target.com/press/release/2020/11/target-and-ulta-beauty-announce-strategic-partners). Supermarkets and big-box stores host Starbucks, McDonald’s, pharmacies, banks, and service providers. But in most cases, store-in-store remains an add-on rather than the dominant logic of the retailer.

That should change.

For retailers, the case is straightforward. Store-in-store can reduce inventory exposure, lower markdown dependence, stabilize inter-store price competition, create more distinctive experiences, and attract brands that want physical presence without building full store networks. It allows retailers to monetize traffic and real estate while limiting the financial damage of bad forecasts.

For brands, the model offers an alternative to the high fixed cost of owned stores. A brand can gain physical access, control presentation, train sales associates, observe demand, and build customer relationships without committing to a standalone set of stores. It can also protect brand equity by reducing the retailer’s incentive to clear inventory through aggressive markdowns. Most importantly, they have the most direct feel for the market pulse, and they have full incentives to do what it takes for the best of their products and consumers.

For consumers, the benefits are just as real and important. Better brand control can mean deeper assortment, better service, fresher inventory, and fewer chaotic end-of-season discount cycles. The customer sees a store that feels more like a curated marketplace than a liquidation machine. Most importantly, consumers will see lower prices when the incentives for channel members are streamlined and aligned and when channel conflicts are avoided.

Managers considering this shift should start with four questions.

First, where is forecast error most expensive? Categories with high fashion risk, short product cycles, complex assortments, or strong brand identities are natural candidates. The more volatile the category, the weaker the case for the retailer to own all inventory risk.

Second, where does brand expertise matter most? Store-in-store works best when manufacturers can genuinely improve assortment, service, and customer education. Cosmetics, luxury, fashion, technology, eyewear, appliances, and specialty categories are strong examples.

Third, what must the retailer still control? Platform retailing is not abdication. Retailers must retain control over brand selection, customer standards, store layout, data governance, conflict rules, and overall experience. The goal is to reallocate risk, not surrender the customer.

Fourth, is inter-store competition becoming ruinous to the detriment of all stakeholders? When all retailers run like a platform, the competitive dynamics in the marketplace change. For instance, LG products on platform A will not want to compete with LG products on platform B, as LG is making merchandising and pricing decisions on both platforms. This will temper inter-store price competition. However, LG will compete harder with Samsung on the same and every platform to get consumers going its way.

The harder challenge is cultural. Many retailers still define merchant skill as the ability to pick winners. That skill will not disappear, but it must evolve. The future merchant will be less like a gambler placing seasonal bets and more like a platform architect: selecting partners, setting incentives, designing rules, allocating space dynamically, and measuring performance across the ecosystem.

A final reason the merchant model is becoming increasingly untenable is the rise of AI-powered buying agents. As consumers delegate more purchasing decisions to algorithms, demand will become more transparent, more price-sensitive, and potentially more volatile. AI agents will compare products, prices, reviews, and delivery options in real time, reducing the influence of traditional merchandising and promotional tactics. This creates a new challenge for retailers operating under the merchant model. Products can rapidly gain or lose favor as AI agents redirect demand, making inventory forecasting even more difficult and increasing the cost of being wrong. Retailers that own inventory will bear these risks directly.

Platform, agency, and store-in-store models provide a more resilient alternative. By shifting inventory ownership and merchandising decisions closer to brands and manufacturers, retailers reduce their exposure to AI-driven demand shocks. As AI transforms shopping, it is likely to accelerate the transition from merchant retailing to platform retailing.

For a century, retail reinvention has often meant a new format entering at the bottom of the wheel: cheaper, leaner, and less encumbered. As AI increasingly shapes both supply and demand, retailers that continue to operate primarily as merchants will find themselves carrying ever greater inventory risk. Those that evolve into platforms—allocating risk to those best equipped to manage it while focusing on traffic, trust, experience, and ecosystem governance—will be positioned to thrive.

kept.heading: SHOW THE COST OF EACH AI PROMPT (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Showing users the cost or remaining capacity of each AI prompt can lead to more intentional usage and better outcomes. #### 👋**We’re back!**

We’re restarting after a 2-week break from the newsletter. My team and I used this time to a) recharge our batteries and b) finalize a few tweaks to make Science Says even better.

The first of which is this new version of our insights! I took your feedback and made tweaks so that they’ll now be leaner, punchier, and go straight to the practical recommendation. I’d love to hear what you think of this new version. Let me know by replying to this email (I read all responses, would to hear what you think!)

Over the next few weeks, expect a couple of more announcements:

*   A new FREE playbook, we’re building with a partner (_to be revealed_) that I’m certain you’ll love

*   A new and improved experience of [our Platform](https://www.sciencesays.com/join-platform?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=show-the-cost-of-each-ai-prompt) with 300+ insights

**Topic**: AI | Pricing

**For**: Both B2C and B2B

**Research date**: April 2026

**Universities**: Indiana University, Pennsylvania State University

#### 📈**Recommendation**

When your team uses AI tools, make sure they know how many tokens they are spending (e.g. a disclaimer saying “you’ve used 8% of your limit””)

If you sell AI tools, show how much capacity has been used, and how much each incremental prompt costs.

People will be more likely to use AI intentionally and will be more satisfied with the output (vs when they think usage is unlimited).

![Image 1](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/f0edcb50-5fea-4cb4-a5e7-609ad2760e00/Insight__338.png?t=1787659829)

#### **🎓 Findings**

*   Researchers tracked 1.8M+ prompts from 61,000+ users and found that when the platform made it clear how much they were consuming (vs a seemingly unlimited plan), people worked:

    *   More intentionally, spending 5% more time on writing prompts, and 8% less on generating variants of the same image

    *   More effectively, being more likely to rewrite and refine prompts (vs resubmitting the same one)

    *   They were also more likely to show signs of satisfaction with the output (e.g. upscaling the image)

*   The effect is stronger among heavy AI users

#### 🧠**Why it works**

*   When we know how much we’re spending, we want more [control](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2016.2643?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=show-the-cost-of-each-ai-prompt) and certainty.

*   So we put more effort into our prompts and work more intentionally.

*   Which makes us feel happier with the outcome.

#### ✋**Limitations**

*   Satisfaction wasn’t directly measured but assumed from the users’ behavior.

*   The study focused on images. The effect might differ for more objective outputs like code. Restricting usage could boost satisfaction through control, or backfire if quality standards aren't met.

#### 👀**Real-life example**

❌**Issue:**Google’s Gemini for enterprise typically has no clear per-user “quotas”. Employees can’t easily track their consumption and see when they reach limits.

✅**Solution:**Google should clarify per-user usage limitations. For example:

*   Give a weekly limit of tokens, and show each person how much they’re using.

*   Alternatively, simply provide an indicative average cost of how much each prompt costs the company.

*   Switch to a more intuitive and less abstract system than “quotas”. Instead, show the number of available prompts that are left. [More intuitive measurements tend to increase sales](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/use-intuitive-measurements).

#### 📖**Research**

_Remember: This is_ _a new_ _scientific discovery. In the future it will probably be better understood and could even be proven wrong (that’s_[how science works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_method?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=show-the-cost-of-each-ai-prompt)_). Title: Affiliate Has Outgrown the Bottom of the Funnel

URL Source: https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/affiliate-marketing-strategy-2027/

Published Time: 2026-08-31T16:10:56+00:00

Markdown Content:
I came away from Affiliate Summit East thinking about an assumption we’ve made about affiliate marketing for years: that its primary job is to capture demand that’s already there.

That made sense when the affiliate journey was easy to see. Someone was considering a purchase, encountered a publisher, comparison site or offer, clicked through and converted. Affiliate sat close to the transaction, so we built programs, budgets and measurement around that role.

But that journey is changing. Consumers now discover and research brands through AI tools, review and comparison sites, Reddit, creators and short-form video, often before they reach a brand’s website. The partners we have traditionally treated as conversion channels are increasingly influencing what people consider in the first place.

I think that changes the job of affiliate. Its opportunity is no longer just to capture demand at the point of conversion, but to help create it. And as that role expands, so must the model around it: where brands invest, how creator and affiliate teams work together, and how we measure the value those partnerships create.

## **Affiliate has to show up before the customer is ready to buy**

The first implication is where affiliate strategy begins.

If someone asks an AI assistant which product to buy, reads a comparison article, watches a creator review and checks Reddit before visiting a brand, a significant amount of consideration has already happened before that brand sees the person as traffic. Those sources may have determined which brands seemed credible or worth investigating at all.

That makes a strategy centered on conversion-adjacent placements too narrow. Coupon and cashback partners still have a role, but they’re only one part of a much larger partner ecosystem. Editorial publishers, comparison sites, reviewers and creators can influence the shortlist much earlier, and that influence becomes particularly important as AI changes how information is discovered and synthesized.

One of my biggest takeaways from the summit was therefore that affiliate teams need to understand where their partners appear during consideration, not only where they appear immediately before conversion. Comparison, review and editorial placements are becoming an important visibility layer as discovery moves further away from brands’ owned properties.

That changes how I think about partner selection too. The question isn’t only whether a partner can efficiently convert someone who is ready to buy. We also need to ask whether they are present in the places customers use to form an opinion, whether audiences trust them and whether they can influence which brands make it into consideration.

## **That makes trust more valuable than traffic alone**

Once affiliate starts influencing consideration, the quality of the audience relationship matters differently. A partner can have enormous reach without having much influence over what its audience actually chooses. Another may have a smaller audience but be one of the sources people actively seek out when they need a recommendation. If we’re evaluating both primarily through traffic and last-click sales, we can easily miss that distinction.

This came through strongly in a summit discussion about publisher trust. The argument was that publishers with genuine, passion-led communities can outperform higher-traffic competitors with shallower audience relationships. There was another interesting wrinkle: in some cases that trust increasingly belongs to an individual writer rather than the publication itself.

Creators make the same point even more clearly. The creator sessions emphasized genuine audience fit over reach and argued that commercially effective partnerships often require brands to give creators enough freedom to retain the authenticity that made their audience trust them in the first place.

For me, that broadens what we’re actually buying when we invest in an affiliate partnership. It isn’t simply access to traffic. We’re investing in someone else’s relationship with an audience, and in their ability to shape a decision. That means partner evaluation has to account for the strength and source of that influence, rather than treating reach as a proxy for it.

## **Creator and affiliate strategies can’t stay separate**

That emphasis on influence exposes another problem: many brands have split the same customer journey across different teams.

Creator or PR teams often manage the people who build awareness and engagement, while affiliate teams manage the people who drive attributable revenue. On paper, the division is tidy. From the customer’s perspective, it increasingly isn’t there.

A creator can introduce someone to a product, explain why it is useful and ultimately drive the purchase. The same relationship can create awareness, consideration and conversion. Yet internally, brands may still run separate creator strategies against separate budgets and objectives, with different approaches to briefing, partner management and measurement.

The summit sessions were particularly clear about the cost of that separation. When PR and affiliate creator activity runs in parallel, budget can be duplicated, attribution breaks down and creator relationships become fragmented. The proposed alternative was to bring both under a coherent strategy with measurement that recognizes value across the funnel.

That becomes even more important as commerce moves onto creator platforms themselves. Shoppable storefronts, live commerce and platform-native shops are making the distance between influence and transaction smaller, while creating new questions around tracking, customer data and who ultimately owns the commercial relationship.

So I don’t think the answer is simply better coordination between creator and affiliate teams. Brands need to start thinking about them as connected parts of the same partnership strategy. The creator who builds demand and the affiliate who converts it may increasingly be the same person.

## **A broader role for affiliate requires broader measurement**

Once affiliate is influencing discovery and consideration, the limitations of last-click measurement become much harder to ignore.

Last click worked particularly well for the version of affiliate we built it to measure. If the channel’s job was to intercept existing demand close to purchase, proximity to the transaction was a reasonable way to assign value. But it tells us far less about a partner whose most important contribution happened earlier.

That creates a practical problem. We can expand affiliate into higher-funnel partnerships, but if we continue evaluating those partnerships against a conversion model designed for the bottom of the funnel, we’ll systematically favor the activity closest to purchase. Eventually, the measurement model pulls the strategy back toward the role we’re trying to move beyond.

That’s why one of the more significant conversations at the summit was around shared data infrastructure. Publishers and affiliate partners are increasingly looking beyond debates about who deserves the final click and toward closer data collaboration with advertisers to understand incremental value. The argument from the session was that this infrastructure can itself become a competitive advantage for partners that build it well.

I think that’s an important shift in mindset. Better affiliate measurement isn’t just about producing a more accurate report at the end of a campaign. It’s what allows brands to invest confidently in partners whose value may show up across discovery, consideration and conversion. If the role of the channel gets broader, the evidence we use to value it has to broaden too.

## **Affiliate is becoming a partnership strategy**

Put all of this together and the bigger change becomes clearer.

Affiliate is still a performance discipline, and its commercial accountability is one of its greatest strengths. But limiting it to the bottom of the funnel increasingly limits what those partnerships can do.

The customer journey now runs through publishers, creators, comparison sites, reviews, AI-generated answers and platform-native commerce. The partners operating across those environments can introduce a brand, build trust, shape consideration and drive a transaction. Treating them purely as the final link in that chain means designing the program around only one part of the value they create.

That was the thread I kept hearing across Affiliate Summit East. One session made the case explicitly for repositioning affiliate as a growth catalyst across the marketing mix rather than a standalone channel competing for budget. I think the shifts happening around discovery, creators and measurement make that argument increasingly difficult to ignore.

The opportunity now is to build affiliate strategies around where and how partners influence customers, then create the structures and measurement needed to value that influence properly. That takes affiliate beyond capturing demand at the end of the journey and gives it a much more interesting role: helping brands create the conditions that make customers choose them in the first place.

kept.heading: AMID GROWING AI DISTRUST, HUMANITY TAKES A FRONT SEAT IN ADVERTISING (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: The growing backlash against AI is prompting brands to make humanity itself a central theme in advertising, either through explicit messaging or more tactile, imperfect creative. Tech brands such as Anthropic and Meta are using optimistic narratives to address concerns about AI, while brands such as Polaroid, Pinterest, and Heineken are encouraging consumers to reconnect with the physical world. Brands can reinforce this positioning through film, handmade aesthetics, natural elements, and behind-the-scenes content that shows real people creating the work. The strategy works best when humanity reflects a genuine point of view rather than becoming another empty brand buzzword.

Title: Amid growing AI distrust, humanity takes a front seat in advertising

URL Source: https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/humanity-in-advertising-ai-distrust

Published Time: 2026-09-01T13:22:38.090Z

Markdown Content:
“What if we started to be more human again?”

A voice poses that question near the end of “Hope in Hard Questions,” a 90-second ad for Anthropic’s Claude. The spot, which debuted earlier this summer, moves through existential quandaries like, “Can AI be trusted?” and “If it ends up taking, like, almost all the jobs, then what does it mean to work?” before taking a more optimistic tone.

In late July, Meta also used techno-optimism in a new ad called “The Future is For Everyone,” albeit set to a [song about the apocalypse](https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/23/meta-launched-a-new-ai-optimism-ad-set-to-a-song-about-human-extinction/). During the 60-second spot, an unseen narrator says Meta is “doubling down” on people “because while technology will change, our intention behind it never will.”

It’s perhaps not surprising that massive tech companies are trying to soothe the [growing concerns](https://www.wsj.com/tech/inside-big-techs-frantic-race-to-quell-the-growing-backlash-to-ai-2a717339?st=CPkDgA&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink) about the negative effects of AI. Cratering [public sentiment](https://www.techbrew.com/stories/ai-data-center-conversation-reaching-fever-pitch), especially when it comes to data centers, has inspired recent [protests](https://www.techbrew.com/stories/dump-big-tech-protests-google-palantir). And when there’s an image problem, after all, it’s marketing’s job to fix it.

But tech companies aren’t alone in putting humanity front and center in advertising messages. Even more comical ads, like Garage Beer and Liquid Death’s recent 90-second musical satire telling audiences to send in their urine to cool off AI data centers, position the move as a way to “save humanity.”

The message that a brand is made by and for humans and will benefit human consumers in some way is not often something that brands have historically been compelled to spell out so explicitly. Marketing experts told us the shift to more overt references to humanity is a reflection of the zeitgeist as the rapid push toward AI adoption and narratives around the tech’s inevitability have led to larger, more existential questions.

“We’re in a cultural moment where it feels like we are not in control,” Megha Parikh, executive strategy director at VML, told us. That reality, she continued, means humanity is “a very powerful message to empower people…You are in charge of your own destiny. I think that’s a really powerful cultural tension that’s playing out in ad land.”

## **Humanity narratives as counterculture**

Marketers are considering those big questions in advertising, recognizing the current moment and reflecting back to consumers what’s on their minds, often positioning the brands with messages of humanity as an alternative to the dominant narrative.

Once you start looking for brand commentary on humanity, it’s easy to spot across industries. [Etsy](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/etsy-life-by-numbers-brand-campaign-celebrate-being-human) and [TD Bank](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/2026/03/03/td-bank-brand-platform-robots-AI-human-connection) have created campaigns touting the human touch, while other brands, including [Polaroid](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/inside-polaroids-pro-analog-marketing-strategy), [Pinterest](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/pinterest-offline-experiential-marketing-strategy), and [Heineken](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/heineken-brand-strategy-community-building), have pitched consumers on getting outside and off their devices, offering a rejection of the current technological landscape.

“We are in a bit of an existential crisis as a society,” Marcus Collins, clinical assistant professor of marketing at the University of Michigan’s Ross School of Business, said, adding that the crisis has prompted questions around what we eat, how we govern and educate, and how we use technology.

He continued: “All these things are being litigated with regard to, What does it mean for humanity? So it’s almost a little tone-deaf to not even have a point of view, and one would argue that the way you engage in culture is by contributing to it, and brands contribute to the cultural discourse by expressing how they see the world.”

Get marketing news you'll actually want to read

Marketing Brew informs marketing pros of the latest on brand strategy, social media, and ad tech via our weekday newsletter, virtual events, marketing conferences, and digital guides.

That’s how Liquid Death and Garage Beer approached the companies’ recent joint ad, which pitched urine produced from drinking their beverages as a savior for humanity.

“There is a lot of anger and anxiety around AI and, in particular, data centers right now,” Andy Pearson, VP of creative at Liquid Death, said. “So we turned it on itself and said, ‘Hey, can we talk about something that everyone is talking about, but in the most Liquid Death way possible?’”

The team landed on a zany spot inspired by ’80s-era messages of idealism and optimism like “Hands Across America,” opting to take a positive tone at a time when many conversations are centered on negative what-ifs.

To Pearson, marketers addressing humanity head-on in advertising is reminiscent of marketers’ recent obsession with authenticity. But it’s a delicate balance to imbue true meaning without making it a meaningless buzzword.

“If we’re having to prove we’re human, it’s sort of like the real-life version of the Captcha stuff,” Pearson said. “Brands are like, ‘We’re humans. We can pick out the two bicycles in this grid of things,’ which is kind of a dark place for us to be at…we have to laugh so you don’t cry.”

## **Human touches**

While some brands are connecting their brands to humanity through explicit messaging, others are implying humanity through aesthetics. [Film](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/2026/02/04/vintage-film-super-bowl-ads-retro-ai-volkswagen-squarespace-instacart), which some brands used for their Super Bowl spots this year, is one increasingly popular choice; others may lean on handmade-feeling elements or make even more subtle choices, like through the use of color.

“The more technology becomes part of our lives, the more we revert back to the things that make us human, whether it’s nature, authenticity, things that are real, and things that you can physically touch,” Laurie Pressman, VP of the Pantone Color Institute, [previously](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/pantone-color-of-the-year-tech-pushback) told Marketing Brew.

Parikh told us VML clients have been asking about “craft” and for the creative to feel “tactile and natural” as well as “imperfect.”

[Behind-the-scenes](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/2025/12/10/ai-alternative-realism-behind-the-scenes-marketing) videos, showing how ads are made, are also becoming more common. Brands like Apple and Coinbase have offered looks into the lengths creative teams will go to when creating their ads, signaling the many ways their brands are made by (and for) humans.

That signal can prompt viewers to feel a new appreciation for the work, which is something Ty Gates, director of communications and marketing for Mother, experienced when watching the behind-the-scenes video for Coinbase’s “Your Way Out” spot.

“I liked it that much more because I knew there were real humans involved in making it,” he said.

As brands figure out how to signal humanity, Collins told us he believes any brand can get in on the trend—if, of course, they have something to say.

“I would say any brand can have a point of view on humanity if they have a point of view,” he said. “The strongest brands transcend the category, so they’re not bound by the industry they’re in and what they make. Instead, they’re freed by the point of view they have on the world.”

kept.heading: TRY GOOGLE PICS: EASY IMAGE CREATION AND EDITING IN GOOGLE WORKSPACE (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Google Pics is an AI image creation and editing tool powered by Google's Nano Banana model. It can generate graphics, edit specific objects, and change text within images. It also creates multiple versions from one prompt. Pics is rolling out to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers and most Workspace business customers. It will also integrate with Docs, Slides, and Drive.

Title: How to Find and Pitch Real Case Studies for Digital PR with Becca Peel

URL Source: https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/case-studies-podcast/

Published Time: 2026-09-01T15:57:41+00:00

*   [Do You Tailor the Case Study for Different Outlets?](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/case-studies-podcast/#Do_You_Tailor_the_Case_Study_for_Different_Outlets "Do You Tailor the Case Study for Different Outlets?")
*   [Do You Prefer Leading With Data or the Case Study?](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/case-studies-podcast/#Do_You_Prefer_Leading_With_Data_or_the_Case_Study "Do You Prefer Leading With Data or the Case Study?")
*   [How Do You Choose Which Journalists to Target?](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/case-studies-podcast/#How_Do_You_Choose_Which_Journalists_to_Target "How Do You Choose Which Journalists to Target?")
*   [Any Final Advice?](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/case-studies-podcast/#Any_Final_Advice "Any Final Advice?")

[Becca Peel](https://www.linkedin.com/in/beccapeelpr/) is the Head of Digital PR at Tank.

She and I met at the Digital PR Summit in Manchester, where we talked about this episode’s topic: case studies for journalists and why they matter so much right now in this age of AI uncertainty, when people aren’t always sure who’s real. It’s causing real problems in our space — but also real opportunities for PRs who are good at this.

*   **AI can gather the data, but it can’t find the human behind it** — that’s exactly why journalists are asking for case studies more than ever.
*   **Start with who you already know** — friends, family, colleagues, or the client’s own network are usually the fastest route to a real case study.
*   **Verify like a journalist would** — LinkedIn, a phone call, a real business footprint — because one fake case study can tank your credibility.
*   **Localize, localize, localize!**Don’t just use the same quote everywhere.
*   **Target journalists who’ve covered people-driven stories before,** not just the beat broadly.
*   Make sure the case study **says something you can’t already Google.**

![Image 1: YouTube player](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/p9FpAT5isM4/maxresdefault.jpg)

Here’s a slightly edited transcript:

## Are Agencies Doing More Case Study Work Now?

**Vince Nero:** Back when we talked in Manchester, I asked what’s really working right now, and one of the things you mentioned was doing a lot more case study work — providing journalists with human stories, real people tied to your campaigns.

That’s not a new idea, but do you feel agencies are leaning into it more these days, or is Tank unusual in that?

**Becca Peel:** It’s definitely not new — I’d say it’s the crux of good journalism.

Watch the BBC now versus ten or twenty years ago: journalists have always needed people to help tell the story, to make it human. But I think digital PR got into a habit of loving data and reports so much that we’d send stories out to press without really humanizing them.

So while the need for that hasn’t changed, journalists are asking for it more — I think because they want exclusivity, something you’re not offering everyone else, and because newsrooms are more time-poor than ever.

There are fewer journalists, and yes, they can use AI to help write a story, but AI can’t find them a real person the story applies to.

A good example: we ran a survey a few weeks ago for a development company about how AI is affecting designers in the US. A couple of publications, including TechRadar — one of the client’s top-tier targets — came back to us, and the journalist said, essentially, “This is great, but we need a case study. We need someone this research actually applies to.”

We’d normally just include a quote from the client, but they wanted to hear from the people the research was actually about.

So even though AI can help with the data gathering and analysis side, that just frees up more time to go find the people journalists actually want to talk to.

## Isn’t Finding Case Studies the Journalist’s Job?

**Vince Nero:** That makes total sense — and it seems so obvious once you say it. I wonder why more people don’t do it.

I’ve talked to others who’ve pushed back and said, “Isn’t that the journalist’s job?”

**Becca Peel:** I get that argument — journalists have always sourced their own case studies or quotes, from councils or elsewhere, when we send them a story.

But it’s also their job to find _a_ story, and if we’re the ones providing it, I don’t see the issue with them asking us to help substantiate it.

It happens the other way too.

The BBC once had a case study of someone whose dog had an allergic reaction because a product’s labeling was wrong, and they needed someone to comment on inaccurate labeling.

We happened to have a client in that space, so we got them into the BBC.

I think it comes down to making sure digital PR is doing right by the brand — and honestly, I think digital PR and traditional PR are becoming the same thing at this point.

**Vince Nero:** I like that — it lets you control more of the narrative and keep the messaging unified if you’ve got your own case study lined up. And journalists are so stretched that if you can hand them almost everything they need — that was one of the first things I learned in this industry — you’re helping your own case too.

## How Do You Actually Find Case Studies?

**Vince Nero:** So how do you actually find these people? You don’t have to give away all your secret sauce, but —

**Becca Peel:** I wish I had just one secret source!

There are so many ways to do this.

The first place we look is our own friends and family, or people at the agency.

For example: we ran a campaign on how much it’s actually costing pub owners and landlords to pour a pint, versus what people assume they’re pocketing when they raise prices to £6.50 or £7.

The data showed they’re barely making anything on it — but to humanize that, one of my team members had a friend who’s a landlord, so we went straight to him.

We’ll also ask around the agency, even people outside our own team, since it’s good for their profile too.

Beyond that: Twitter, and ResponseSource, which a lot of journalists use to source quotes — we respond to those requests, but we also use it to find case studies by working with other companies’ PRs.

Sometimes it’s through the client directly. For a “save the bees” campaign, we researched where bees are struggling most in the UK, and it turned out our client knew a beekeeper with her own farm — a perfect case study.

I’ve even been a case study myself once, for a campaign that wasn’t even ours — I saw a request and thought, “that’s me, I can help.”

And sometimes you have to get resourceful: cold-emailing businesses that fit the criteria if you don’t already know anyone.

**Vince Nero:** So you’re putting on your journalist hat.

**Becca Peel:** Exactly — you’re doing a bit of journalism yourself.

It takes time, but it’s actually fun, and you end up with a story nobody else can tell, because you’ve got that insight and access. Start with people you know, or even yourself. For a campaign about ADHD and neurodiversity tax on spending, we knew someone at the agency who’s open about having ADHD, so they became the case study.

It really is about who you know, who the client knows, and then putting on that journalist hat.

**Vince Nero:** I love that AI can take over the parts it’s good at, so you can spend your time on the part it can’t do.

## Is There Such a Thing as a Bad Case Study?

**Vince Nero:** Do you think there’s such a thing as a bad case study? How do you gauge whether something’s going to resonate — is it about gathering multiple sources, or is one strong person enough?

**Becca Peel:** With everything going on right now — people literally inventing fake case studies, which still blows my mind — you have to be able to substantiate that the person is real.

Photos help.

Being able to actually talk to the person on the phone helps even more, or seeing they’re linked to a real business.

It’s about doing your due diligence to make sure what they’re saying is true, and that it still fits the brand you’re representing.

You wouldn’t want a case study from a competitor, or someone whose messaging clashes with the client’s. It comes back to doing PR properly — the way journalists would expect.

## Do You Steer the Case Study Toward the Story You Want?

**Vince Nero:** Right — like with the beekeeper example, you’re probably going in with an idea of what you want them to say.

Do you draft questions ahead of time to steer toward the story?

**Becca Peel:** That’s a good point.

If we built a campaign around data saying one thing and a case study then contradicted it, that would be a problem — thankfully that hasn’t happened yet, hopefully because our campaigns are solid to begin with. We do draft questions in advance, sometimes hop on a call like this one to save everyone time, and we always run the final piece by them before publishing.

If someone’s answer genuinely didn’t match the data, we’d have to go back and look at the data again, or just use a different part of the quote.

It’s a fair concern, but we’re not manipulating the story — we’re finding someone whose real experience matches an outcome we’ve already found in the data.

If our survey shows designers are worried about AI taking their jobs, we go find a designer who’s genuinely grappling with that. We’re not putting words in anyone’s mouth, just finding someone whose story fits.

**Vince Nero:** Right — you’re not just asking a random designer what they think; you’re finding someone who’s actually been affected.

I think that’s what gives a case study its emotional angle, or doubles down on whatever emotion the data already points to.

**Becca Peel:** Exactly — and it works. When we ran the pub landlord story, the version with the case study as the headline was the one that got picked up and shared, and it got thousands of interactions on social media — way more than the other angles from the same campaign. People relate to people.

## Is This Common Outside the UK?

**Vince Nero:** Is this a US thing too, or mostly UK?

**Becca Peel:** It’s pretty universal at this point. We work with a food intolerance company in the US, and we get a lot of requests there too — people who’ve experienced celiac disease or other intolerances, on top of an expert quote from the client.

I’ve been doing this about ten years, and I’ve never had journalists ask for case studies as often as they do now.

Newsrooms are stretched thin and need to make sure people are actually reading their stories, so they need that human angle, and something exclusive.

We usually offer the case study as an exclusive first, then work a version of the quote into the wider release.

In the US especially, there’s a strong appetite for it around broadcast and local news — outlets won’t always interview the person on camera, but they’ll use their photo and tell the story through local news sites.

**Vince Nero:** That tracks — local news is still a big deal here, even as it shrinks.

I’ve talked to producers who say you need people ready to go.

I’ve had a guest on this podcast whose phone started ringing mid-interview because a local station wanted him to comment on something, just because he’d become a go-to voice.

## How Do You Verify a Case Study Is Real?

**Vince Nero:** Given all the fake case studies floating around right now — like the “Royal Cleaner” story, which I think started with a UK outlet, though I won’t point fingers without being sure — how do you verify someone before you put them forward?

**Becca Peel:** Beyond talking to them directly, you want to see they’ve got a real footprint: a website if relevant, a Google listing for their business, LinkedIn, contactable information.

Our beekeeper, for instance, had already been on the news herself, so we knew she was real.

That said, I’ve seen investigations into fake “experts” who even had fabricated LinkedIn profiles, which is wild.

I always try to get on a call with case studies myself. And increasingly, journalists are asking to speak directly to our expert spokespeople too — not just the case study — and asking for quotes to come straight from them, which we obviously coordinate, but it’s another trust signal for the journalist.

Basically: check every box you can. Do they have LinkedIn? Have you spoken to them on the phone?

Do they have a real location listed on Google? A website? Have they appeared in the media before? A lot of people who respond to our ResponseSource call-outs have been in the press before, which helps verify them too.

And any other trust signal helps — we had a small-business case study who’d appeared on Dragons’ Den, and another who’d been on The Apprentice.

You don’t need a huge trust signal like that, but it helps both with coverage and with verification.

**Vince Nero:** That’s a great point — back when I did more of this myself, part of the reason to line up expert commentary strategically was SEO: if you found someone with a high-authority blog or a strong social following, there was a good chance they’d link back to the piece or share it.

**Becca Peel:** That’s a great point too.

**Vince Nero:** So it seems like the same checks you’re doing for authenticity also tend to double as strengths — if they’ve got a blog, they might link to it; if they’ve got a following, they might share it. Verifying someone properly ends up paying off twice.

**Becca Peel:** Exactly. I can’t think of anything worse than accidentally putting out a fake comment. It’s wild that this is even something we have to think about now.

## Do You Include a Case Study in Every Pitch?

**Vince Nero:** Do you include a case study proactively in every pitch?

**Becca Peel:** I’d say eight times out of ten.

For reactive work — say, a fast-turnaround story like a new Prime Minister being announced — we usually won’t have time to line one up unless a journalist specifically asks. But for planned campaigns, yes: bringing a case study along gives us an extra layer to go out with, and it means every release can include that quote.

It takes more planning up front — thinking early about who we know, who the client knows, or who someone else might know — but it’s worth it.

**Vince Nero:** That could easily be the thing that makes a pitch stand out.

## Do You Tailor the Case Study for Different Outlets?

**Vince Nero:** Do you use the same case study for every outlet, or tailor it?

**Becca Peel:** We tailor it. For a typical campaign we’ll have six or seven different press releases.

There’s the overarching national release built around the top-line stats, which might include a short quote from the case study.

Then we’ll write standalone releases built entirely around the case study — for the beekeeper campaign, for example, a release headlined around her warning about Asian hornets, which apparently eat dozens of bees a day and are a real threat to hives (I hadn’t known about that until she mentioned it).

For the pub story, it was a landlord calling on the government to act, tied back into our data.

We’ll also localize it — the pub landlord release went out nationally with a quote, but we also built a separate, hyper-local release for their specific town.

If it had come from the client instead, it would still land, but the client isn’t the one living the situation — the case study is.

**Vince Nero:** Right — as a journalist, you’d probably lead a human-interest piece with the person, and bring in the data to support it, rather than the other way around.

## Do You Prefer Leading With Data or the Case Study?

**Becca Peel:** Exactly. I studied journalism at university, so I’m biased toward leading with the case study, though for mass coverage, leading with data still works.

But it’s shifting — there’s so much data out there that says nothing on its own.

I think that’s a real risk in digital PR: analyzing a pile of data and going out with a story that doesn’t actually say anything.

You have to find the story in the numbers first.

**Vince Nero:** I’ve seen that too — cases where the data was solid, but what actually landed the coverage was the human impact of it.

## How Do You Choose Which Journalists to Target?

**Vince Nero:** Let’s talk about the media list side. Are there particular signals you look for in a journalist?

**Becca Peel:** People keep bringing up your Digital PR Summit talk about making sure you’re targeting the right journalists — not just someone who covers “sports” broadly, but someone who specifically covers, say, cricket, and covers it from an angle that fits your story rather than sports politics or something unrelated.

Journalists who cover people-driven stories tend to be a bit easier to spot.

One of my first-ever case study pitches was for an NHS discount card company: we found two women who’d met working as paramedics and fallen in love, and tied it to Valentine’s Day.

We sent it as an exclusive on a Friday morning, to journalists I’d spent the morning identifying — checking the Daily Mirror, The Sun, The Guardian for journalists who’d written that kind of first-person story before; sometimes you can even see it in their quotes or headlines. Almost every journalist we sent it to said yes, because people like people.

The same logic applies to any media list: research who’s covered similar first-person stories before, and target accordingly. I wouldn’t send a beekeeper story to a music publication.

**Vince Nero:** That maps to your talk — you’re finding the people who’ve clearly done human-interest stories first, and then a second wave for the data-focused angle.

**Becca Peel:** Right — and once a case study quote is out there in a bigger story, it’s essentially spent.

I had a journalist at The Guardian tell me a case study we’d pitched might make the weekend edition, then come back a few hours later to say someone else had already covered it, so they couldn’t.

Frustrating, but it’s pushed us to prioritize whoever we’re closest to publishing next: they don’t need a case study locked as an exclusive forever, but they do need to be first. As we build relationships, we log strong responses into our tier-one media lists — I won’t pitch the same journalist every time, but I’m also not turning down The Guardian three times in a row.

**Vince Nero:** That relationship-building matters — it’s not only about the coverage on any single pitch.

**Becca Peel:** Exactly — they’ll come back to you too. We have a journalist at Ideal Home who comes back to us every single month now for quotes from one of our flower clients.

## Any Final Advice?

**Vince Nero:** Becca, anything we didn’t cover that you’d want to leave people with?

**Becca Peel:** Just: make sure you’re saying something new.

There’s a journalist, Rob Waugh from Press Gazette, who said something that stuck with me — if you can Google it and it’s already out there, it shouldn’t be in the story.

That applies just as much to case studies. You can’t dictate what someone says, but you can ask questions that help them say something genuinely new.

And if they have a real USP — they’ve been on Dragons’ Den, they’ve won an award, they keep bees, they run their own farm — lean into it.

It helps you cut through, and it helps verification too. A generic case study from just anyone won’t cut through with journalists who are this stretched for time.

**Vince Nero:** Rob actually said that same line on this podcast — maybe that’s where you picked it up, or maybe it’s just his catchphrase. Either way, great advice.

I think the bigger theme here is putting yourself in the journalist’s shoes. With a journalism background, that probably comes more naturally to you — the rest of us learn it the hard way, through a lot of rejected pitches.

## Vince Nero

Vince is the Director of Content Marketing at Buzzstream. He thinks content marketers should solve for users, not just Google. He also loves finding creative content online. His previous work includes content marketing agency Siege Media for six years, Homebuyer.com, and The Grit Group. Outside of work, you can catch Vince running, playing with his 2 kids, enjoying some video games, or watching Phillies baseball.

To answer shoppers’ questions in real time, the company created an [AI](https://www.fastcompany.com/section/artificial-intelligence "AI") tool called E.l.f.luencer—trained on the company’s stylebook and years of human-written social comments—that autogenerates responses to comments left by consumers on social media platforms.

The comments are approved by human community managers before being posted, part of the company’s “human-first, human-last strategy.” “The tool saved a lot of time [for community managers],” says Ekta Chopra, the company’s chief technology and AI officer. “Our response rate was like 30%-40% before launching E.l.f.luencer. Fast forward, it’s gone above 80%; 90% of the comments are generated by AI in our brand tone, using the language and emojis E.l.f is known for. ” Chopra adds that artificial intelligence at the company is used to augment [productivity](https://www.fastcompany.com/section/productivity "Productivity"), but all outputs are closely reviewed by human employees.

This is just one initiative Chopra, a 10-year E.l.f. veteran, has overseen. In her role, Chopra helps the company identify and implement its AI ambitions. To oversee AI implementation across the company, Chopra created a cross-functional AI steering committee spanning legal, [marketing](https://www.fastcompany.com/section/marketing "Marketing"), and R&D with the goal of moving most agentic AI pilots into full production within six months and minimizing risks associated with the technology. Under her leadership, the company is piloting 85 agentic AI use cases. Her deep investment in using AI across departments has helped E.l.f create internal tools and consumer-facing tools like E.l.f.luencer.

Internally, Chopra has created AI tools to streamline processes and distribute information at every level of the company. There’s an internal chatbot called “B.F.e.l.f” that is used by more than 80% of employees. There’s also an IT help desk assistant called “e.l.f.line” that the company says can accomplish support work equivalent to that of one human help desk employee. Additional internal applications include tools to help products get surfaced by large language models when people search anything on the internet, as SEO continues to deliver fewer returns.

To accomplish all of this, Chopra created a secure internal AI platform available to every employee that provides approved connectors and APIs, allowing nontechnical staff to build their own agents or apps and deploy them without relying on a central tech team. “We want to democratize that access for “e.l.f.z” (E.l.f. employees) because they’re closest to the work and they can really reimagine that work,” Chopra says. Among the tools employees have built is a dashboard that tracks social sentiment across campaigns and products.

Title: OpenAI’s Astra model is on the way — and very good at breaking into computer systems

URL Source: https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/01/open-ais-astra-model-is-on-the-way-and-very-good-at-breaking-into-computer-systems/

Published Time: 2026-09-01T21:06:24+00:00

Markdown Content:
OpenAI [shared new details](https://openai.com/index/path-to-astra/) on its forthcoming Astra model, which the company said is the first large language model to meet its “critical cybersecurity threshold,” in preparation for its imminent release.

“We plan to make Astra available soon,” OpenAI’s blog post reads, “but access to its most advanced cybersecurity capabilities will be more limited.”

The frontier lab determined that Astra is capable of finding unknown security flaws in computer systems, and exploiting them without a person’s guidance. That’s similar to the concerns Anthropic raised about its Mythos model earlier this year, and OpenAI is taking comparable precautions as it prepares to roll out the Astra.

Without any third-party confirmation, it is difficult to evaluate OpenAI’s claims about safety or preparedness. The company said it would preview the model with a group of testers but did not say who they were or how they would be chosen. It’s not clear if OpenAI is working with the U.S. government to evaluate the model ahead of release.

OpenAI noted that Astra scored a perfect score on ExploitBench, an evaluation of an LLM’s ability to hack into known system vulnerabilities. In a modified version of the test developed by OpenAI engineers, the model discovered and exploited two zero-day vulnerabilities, the company said.

To ensure that its models are neither exploited by bad actors nor capable of bad behavior itself, OpenAI said it had already begun improving the model’s harness to detect abuses and prevent jailbreaks.

For Astra, however, the company invested in unspecified new techniques designed to make the model safer. OpenAI has also started identifying “accounts assessed as higher risk” and restricting the model’s responses to their prompts, though it also doesn’t say how. Finally, though the company describes Astra as its “most aligned model to date,” it will deploy the model with additional chain-of-thought monitoring to spot and stop bad behavior.

Preparations for the release of Astra come as the industry reacts to OpenAI agents breaking out of a training environment and accessing private data on Hugging Face, a popular model and benchmark distribution platform.

For Astra, OpenAI said it designed a test to tempt the new model to replicate the actions of the rogue agents in the Hugging Face incident, which collaborated to access the open internet despite safeguards applied by OpenAI researchers. They said Astra did not attempt to break out of its testing environment in these experiments.

Yona Shavit, a former OpenAI employee who now works on AI resilience at the OpenAI Foundation, [wondered on social media](https://x.com/yonashav/status/2094887195249168609?s=20) whether Astra’s unwillingness to break the rules may have resulted from knowing what was expected of it or trying to fool researchers.

And for all these new details, it’s still difficult to know exactly what Astra is capable of or if OpenAI is taking the right measures to ensure safety. The company said it expects to release more evaluations of the model and further safety information when it is launched widely to the public.

At that point, however, the cat will be out of the bag.
